“What a number of bond robberies there have been lately!” I observed
one morning, laying aside the newspaper. “Poirot, let us forsake
the science of detection, and take to crime instead!”

“You are on the—how do you say it?—get-rich-quick tack, eh, _mon
ami_?”

“Well, look at this last _coup_, the million dollars’ worth of
Liberty Bonds which the London and Scottish Bank were sending to
New York, and which disappeared in such a remarkable manner on
board the _Olympia_.”

“If it were not for the _mal de mer_, and the difficulty of
practising the so excellent method of Laverguier for a longer time
than the few hours of crossing the channel, I should delight to
voyage myself on one of these big liners,” murmured Poirot dreamily.

“Yes, indeed,” I said enthusiastically. “Some of them must be
perfect palaces; the swimming-baths, the lounges, the restaurant,
the palm courts—really, it must be hard to believe that one is on
the sea.”

“Me, I always know when I am on the sea,” said Poirot sadly. “And
all those bagatelles that you enumerate, they say nothing to me;
but, my friend, consider for a moment the geniuses that travel as
it were incognito! On board these floating palaces, as you so
justly call them, one would meet the élite, the _haute noblesse_
of the criminal world!”

I laughed.

“So that’s the way your enthusiasm runs! You would have liked to
cross swords with the man who sneaked the Liberty Bonds?”

The landlady interrupted us.

“A young lady as wants to see you, Mr. Poirot. Here’s her card.”

The card bore the inscription: Miss Esmée Farquhar, and Poirot,
after diving under the table to retrieve a stray crumb, and putting
it carefully in the waste-paper-basket, nodded to the landlady to
admit her.

In another minute one of the most charming girls I have ever seen
was ushered into the room. She was perhaps about five-and-twenty,
with big brown eyes and a perfect figure. She was well-dressed and
perfectly composed in manner.

“Sit down, I beg of you, mademoiselle. This is my friend, Captain
Hastings, who aids me in my little problems.”

“I am afraid it is a big problem I have brought you to-day, Monsieur
Poirot,” said the girl, giving me a pleasant bow as she seated
herself. “I dare say you have read about it in the papers. I am
referring to the theft of Liberty Bonds on the _Olympia_.” Some
astonishment must have shown itself in Poirot’s face, for she
continued quickly: “You are doubtless asking yourself what I have
to do with a grave institution like the London and Scottish Bank.
In one sense nothing, in another sense everything. You see, Monsieur
Poirot, I am engaged to Mr. Philip Ridgeway.”

“Aha! and Mr. Philip Ridgeway——”

“Was in charge of the bonds when they were stolen. Of course no
actual blame can attach to him, it was not his fault in any way.
Nevertheless, he is half distraught over the matter, and his uncle,
I know, insists that he must carelessly have mentioned having them
in his possession. It is a terrible set-back in his career.”

“Who is his uncle?”

“Mr. Vavasour, joint general manager of the London and Scottish
Bank.”

“Suppose, Miss Farquhar, that you recount to me the whole story?”

“Very well. As you know, the Bank wished to extend their credits
in America, and for this purpose decided to send over a million
dollars in Liberty Bonds. Mr. Vavasour selected his nephew, who
had occupied a position of trust in the Bank for many years and
who was conversant with all the details of the Bank’s dealings in
New York, to make the trip. The Olympia sailed from Liverpool on
the 23rd, and the bonds were handed over to Philip on the morning
of that day by Mr. Vavasour and Mr. Shaw, the two joint general
managers of the London and Scottish Bank. They were counted,
enclosed in a package, and sealed in his presence, and he then
locked the package at once in his portmanteau.”

“A portmanteau with an ordinary lock?”

“No, Mr. Shaw insisted on a special lock being fitted to it by
Hubbs’s. Philip, as I say, placed the package at the bottom of the
trunk. It was stolen just a few hours before reaching New York. A
rigorous search of the whole ship was made, but without result.
The bonds seemed literally to have vanished into thin air.”

Poirot made a grimace.

“But they did not vanish absolutely, since I gather that they were
sold in small parcels within half an hour of the docking of the
_Olympia_! Well, undoubtedly the next thing is for me to see Mr.
Ridgeway.”

“I was about to suggest that you should lunch with me at the
‘Cheshire Cheese.’ Philip will be there. He is meeting me, but does
not yet know that I have been consulting you on his behalf.”

We agreed to this suggestion readily enough, and drove there in a
taxi.

Mr. Philip Ridgeway was there before us, and looked somewhat
surprised to see his fiancée arriving with two complete strangers.
He was a nice-looking young fellow, tall and spruce, with a touch
of greying hair at the temples, though he could not have been much
over thirty.

Miss Farquhar went up to him and laid her hand on his arm.

“You must forgive my acting without consulting you, Philip,” she
said. “Let me introduce you to Monsieur Hercule Poirot, of whom
you must often have heard, and his friend, Captain Hastings.”

Ridgeway looked very astonished.

“Of course I have heard of you, Monsieur Poirot,” he said, as he
shook hands. “But I had no idea that Esmée was thinking of
consulting you about my—our trouble.”

“I was afraid you would not let me do it, Philip,” said Miss
Farquhar meekly.

“So you took care to be on the safe side,” he observed, with a
smile. “I hope Monsieur Poirot will be able to throw some light on
this extraordinary puzzle, for I confess frankly that I am nearly
out of my mind with worry and anxiety about it.”

Indeed, his face looked drawn and haggard and showed only too
clearly the strain under which he was labouring.

“Well, well,” said Poirot. “Let us lunch, and over lunch we will
put our heads together and see what can be done. I want to hear
Mr. Ridgeway’s story from his own lips.”

Whilst we discussed the excellent steak and kidney pudding of the
establishment, Philip Ridgeway narrated the circumstances leading
to the disappearance of the bonds. His story agreed with that of
Miss Farquhar in every particular. When he had finished, Poirot
took up the thread with a question.

“What exactly led you to discover that the bonds had been stolen,
Mr. Ridgeway?”

He laughed rather bitterly.

“The thing stared me in the face, Monsieur Poirot. I couldn’t have
missed it. My cabin trunk was half out from under the bunk and all
scratched and cut about where they’d tried to force the lock.”

“But I understood that it had been opened with a key?”

“That’s so. They tried to force it, but couldn’t. And, in the end,
they must have got it unlocked somehow or other.”

“Curious,” said Poirot, his eyes beginning to flicker with the
green light I knew so well. “Very curious! They waste much, much
time trying to prise it open, and then—_sapristi!_ they find that
they have the key all the time—for each of Hubbs’s locks are
unique.”

“That’s just why they couldn’t have had the key. It never left me
day or night.”

“You are sure of that?”

“I can swear to it, and besides, if they had had the key or a
duplicate, why should they waste time trying to force an obviously
unforceable lock?”

“Ah! there is exactly the question we are asking ourselves! I
venture to prophesy that the solution, if we ever find it, will
hinge on that curious fact. I beg of you not to assault me if I
ask you one more question: _Are you perfectly certain you did not
leave the trunk unlocked?_”

Philip Ridgeway merely looked at him, and Poirot gesticulated
apologetically.

“Ah, but these things can happen, I assure you! Very well, the
bonds were stolen from the trunk. What did the thief do with them?
How did he manage to get ashore with them?”

“Ah!” cried Ridgeway. “That’s just it. How? Word was passed to the
Customs authorities, and every soul that left the ship was gone
over with a toothcomb!”

“And the bonds, I gather, made a bulky package?”

“Certainly they did. They could hardly have been hidden on board—and
anyway we know they weren’t because they were offered for sale
within half an hour of the _Olympia’s_ arrival, long before I got
the cables going and the numbers sent out. One broker swears he
bought some of them even before the _Olympia_ got in. But you can’t
send bonds by wireless.”

“Not by wireless, but did any tug come alongside?”

“Only the official ones, and that was after the alarm was given
when every one was on the look-out. I was watching out myself for
their being passed over to some one that way. My God, Monsieur
Poirot, this thing will drive me mad! People are beginning to say
I stole them myself.”

“But you also were searched on landing, weren’t you?” asked Poirot
gently.

“Yes.”

The young man stared at him in a puzzled manner.

“You do not catch my meaning, I see,” said Poirot, smiling
enigmatically. “Now I should like to make a few inquiries at the
Bank.”

Ridgeway produced a card and scribbled a few words on it.

“Send this in and my uncle will see you at once.”

Poirot thanked him, bade farewell to Miss Farquhar, and together
we started out for Threadneedle Street and the head office of the
London and Scottish Bank. On production of Ridgeway’s card, we were
led through the labyrinth of counters and desks, skirting paying-in
clerks and paying-out clerks and up to a small office on the first
floor where the joint general managers received us. They were two
grave gentlemen, who had grown grey in the service of the Bank.
Mr. Vavasour had a short white beard, Mr. Shaw was clean shaven.

“I understand you are strictly a private inquiry agent?” said Mr.
Vavasour. “Quite so, quite so. We have, of course, placed ourselves
in the hands of Scotland Yard. Inspector McNeil has charge of the
case. A very able officer, I believe.”

“I am sure of it,” said Poirot politely. “You will permit a few
questions, on your nephew’s behalf? About this lock, who ordered
it from Hubbs’s?”

“I ordered it myself,” said Mr. Shaw. “I would not trust to any
clerk in the matter. As to the keys, Mr. Ridgeway had one, and the
other two are held by my colleague and myself.”

“And no clerk has had access to them?”

Mr. Shaw turned inquiringly to Mr. Vavasour. “I think I am correct
in saying that they have remained in the safe where we placed them
on the 23rd,” said Mr. Vavasour. “My colleague was unfortunately
taken ill a fortnight ago—in fact on the very day that Philip left
us. He has only just recovered.”

“Severe bronchitis is no joke to a man of my age,” said Mr. Shaw
ruefully. “But I am afraid Mr. Vavasour has suffered from the hard
work entailed by my absence, especially with this unexpected worry
coming on top of everything.”

Poirot asked a few more questions. I judged that he was endeavouring
to gauge the exact amount of intimacy between uncle and nephew.
Mr. Vavasour’s answers were brief and punctilious. His nephew was
a trusted official of the Bank, and had no debts or money
difficulties that he knew of. He had been entrusted with similar
missions in the past. Finally we were politely bowed out.

“I am disappointed,” said Poirot, as we emerged into the street.

“You hoped to discover more? They are such stodgy old men.”

“It is not their stodginess which disappoints me, _mon ami_. I do
not expect to find in a Bank manager a ‘keen financier with an
eagle glance’ as your favourite works of fiction put it. No, I am
disappointed in the case—it is too easy!”

“Easy?”

“Yes, do you not find it almost childishly simple?”

“You know who stole the bonds?”

“I do.”

“But then—we must—why——”

“Do not confuse and fluster yourself, Hastings. We are not going
to do anything at present.”

“But why? What are you waiting for?”

“For the _Olympia_. She is due on her return trip from New York on
Tuesday.”

“But if you know who stole the bonds, why wait? He may escape.”

“To a South Sea island where there is no extradition? No, _mon
ami_, he would find life very uncongenial there. As to why I
wait—_eh bien_ to the intelligence of Hercule Poirot the case is
perfectly clear, but for the benefit of others, not so greatly
gifted by the good God—the Inspector McNeil, for instance—it would
be as well to make a few inquiries to establish the facts. One must
have consideration for those less gifted than oneself.”

“Good Lord, Poirot! Do you know, I’d give a considerable sum of
money to see you make a thorough ass of yourself—just for once.
You’re so confoundedly conceited!”

“Do not enrage yourself, Hastings. In verity, I observe that there
are times when you almost detest me! Alas, I suffer the penalties
of greatness!”

The little man puffed out his chest, and sighed so comically that
I was forced to laugh.

Tuesday saw us speeding to Liverpool in a first-class carriage of
the L. & N.W.R. Poirot had obstinately refused to enlighten me as
to his suspicions—or certainties. He contented himself with
expressing surprise that I, too, was not equally _au fait_ with
the situation. I disdained to argue, and entrenched my curiosity
behind a rampart of pretended indifference.

Once arrived at the quay alongside which lay the big transatlantic
liner, Poirot became brisk and alert. Our proceedings consisted in
interviewing four successive stewards and inquiring after a friend
of Poirot’s who had crossed to New York on the 23rd.

“An elderly gentleman, wearing glasses. A great invalid, hardly
moved out of his cabin.”

The description appeared to tally with one Mr. Ventnor who had
occupied the cabin C 24 which was next to that of Philip Ridgeway.
Although unable to see how Poirot had deduced Mr. Ventnor’s
existence and personal appearance, I was keenly excited.

“Tell me,” I cried, “was this gentleman one of the first to land
when you got to New York?” The steward shook his head.

“No, indeed, sir, he was one of the last off the boat.”

I retired crestfallen, and observed Poirot grinning at me. He
thanked the steward, a note changed hands, and we took our
departure.

“It’s all very well,” I remarked heatedly, “but that last answer
must have damped your precious theory, grin as you please!”

“As usual, you see nothing, Hastings. That last answer is, on the
contrary, the coping-stone of my theory.”

I flung up my hands in despair.

“I give it up.”

When we were in the train, speeding towards London, Poirot wrote
busily for a few minutes, sealing up the result in an envelope.

“This is for the good Inspector McNeil. We will leave it at Scotland
Yard in passing, and then to the Rendezvous Restaurant, where I
have asked Miss Esmée Farquhar to do us the honour of dining with
us.”

“What about Ridgeway?”

“What about him?” asked Poirot with a twinkle.

“Why, you surely don’t think—you can’t——”

“The habit of incoherence is growing upon you, Hastings. As a
matter of fact I _did_ think. If Ridgeway had been the thief—which
was perfectly possible—the case would have been charming; a piece
of neat methodical work.”

“But not so charming for Miss Farquhar.”

“Possibly you are right. Therefore all is for the best. Now,
Hastings, let us review the case. I can see that you are dying to
do so. The sealed package is removed from the trunk and vanishes,
as Miss Farquhar puts it, into thin air. We will dismiss the thin
air theory, which is not practicable at the present stage of
science, and consider what is likely to have become of it. Every
one asserts the incredibility of its being smuggled ashore——”

“Yes, but we know——”

“_You_ may know, Hastings. I do not. I take the view that, since
it seemed incredible, it _was_ incredible. Two possibilities
remain: it was hidden on board—also rather difficult—or it was
thrown overboard.”

“With a cork on it, do you mean?”

“Without a cork.”

I stared.

“But if the bonds were thrown overboard, they couldn’t have been
sold in New York.”

“I admire your logical mind, Hastings. The bonds were sold in New
York, therefore they were not thrown overboard. You see where that
leads us?”

“Where we were when we started.”

“_Jamais de la vie!_ If the package was thrown overboard, and the
bonds were sold in New York, the package could not have contained
the bonds. Is there any evidence that the package _did_ contain
the bonds? Remember, Mr. Ridgeway never opened it from the time it
was placed in his hands in London.”

“Yes, but then——”

Poirot waved an impatient hand.

“Permit me to continue. The last moment that the bonds are seen as
bonds is in the office of the London and Scottish Bank on the
morning of the 23rd. They reappear in New York half an hour after
the _Olympia_ gets in, and according to one man, whom nobody
listens to, actually _before_ she gets in. Supposing then, that
they have never been on the _Olympia_ at all? Is there any other
way they could get to New York? Yes. The _Gigantic_ leaves
Southampton on the same day as the _Olympia_, and she holds the
record for the Atlantic. Mailed by the _Gigantic_, the bonds would
be in New York the day before the _Olympia_ arrived. All is clear,
the case begins to explain itself. The sealed packet is only a
dummy, and the moment of its substitution must be in the office in
the Bank. It would be an easy matter for any of the three men
present to have prepared a duplicate package which could be
substituted for the genuine one. _Très bien_, the bonds are mailed
to a confederate in New York, with instructions to sell as soon as
the _Olympia_ is in, but some one must travel on the _Olympia_ to
engineer the supposed moment of the robbery.”

“But why?”

“Because if Ridgeway merely opens the packet and finds it a dummy,
suspicion flies at once to London. No, the man on board in the
cabin next door does his work, pretends to force the lock in an
obvious manner so as to draw immediate attention to the theft,
really unlocks the trunk with a duplicate key, throws the package
overboard and waits until the last to leave the boat. Naturally he
wears glasses to conceal his eyes, and is an invalid since he does
not want to run the risk of meeting Ridgeway. He steps ashore in
New York and returns by the first boat available.”

“But who—which was he?”

“The man who had a duplicate key, the man who ordered the lock,
the man who has _not_ been severely ill with bronchitis at his home
in the country—_enfin_, that ‘stodgy’ old man, Mr. Shaw! There are
criminals in high places sometimes, my friend. Ah, here we are.
Mademoiselle, I have succeeded! You permit?”

And, beaming, Poirot kissed the astonished girl lightly on either
cheek!

He had the only two keys in existence—or so he thought—and they were both on his person at the time.”

“Thin air! That is a phrase of the most romantic, mademoiselle, but it does not satisfy the little grey cells. In this world of ours, things do not vanish without human agency. Tell me, who had the keys to this famous portmanteau?”

“Nothing vanishes into thin air, mademoiselle,” he remarked. “There is always a way, though it be not immediately apparent. Tell me more of the voyage. The portmanteau, it was in Mr. Ridgeway’s cabin, I presume? And the keys—who had the keys?”

“Thin air! They do not vanish, the bonds of Liberty. They are too
solid, too substantial for that. Tell me, mademoiselle, did Mr.
Ridgeway have the key always on his person? And where is he now?
Can I not see him myself?”

“He is outside in a taxi,” replied the girl. “He was so—so ashamed
of his failure that I had the greatest difficulty in persuading him
to come at all. I will fetch him.”

“Thin air! It is an expression that I do not like,” said Poirot, shaking his head. “Things do not vanish into thin air; they are moved from one place to another. Tell me, Mademoiselle, what of the key to this portmanteau? Did your Monsieur Ridgeway keep it in his pocket, or was it perhaps under his pillow while he slept?”

“But they did not vanish absolutely, since I gather that they were
sold in small parcels within half an hour of the docking of the
_Olympia_! Well, undoubtedly the next thing is for me to see Mr.
Ridgeway.”

“I was about to suggest that you should lunch with me at the
‘Cheshire Cheese.’ Philip will be there. He is meeting me, but does
not yet know that I have been consulting you on his behalf.”

We agreed to this suggestion readily enough, and drove there in a
taxi.

“It is very kind of you,” said Ridgeway, “but I fear it is a hopeless business. The police on both sides of the Atlantic are completely baffled. They have searched the ship from stem to stern, and every passenger as well.” Poirot smiled. “The police, they look for the thing that is hidden; I look for the thing that is plain. Tell me, Monsieur Ridgeway, exactly when did you last see the bonds in the trunk?”

“It is the best thing she could have done,” said Poirot. “Believe me, Monsieur Ridgeway, I have a great deal of experience in these matters. Tell me now, the whole story, from the moment you received the bonds at the Bank.” Ridgeway sighed, his face clouding over. “There is very little to tell, but what there is, is baffling to the last degree. On the morning of the twenty-third, I went to the Bank by appointment. Mr. Vavasour and Mr. Shaw were both present. The bonds were counted before me, placed in a large manila envelope, and then into the portmanteau which, as Esmée told you, had been fitted with a special lock. I saw it locked, and the key remained in my pocket from that moment until I reached my cabin on the _Olympia_.”

“It is very kind of you,” said Ridgeway, “though I fear you will find it a thankless task. The whole thing is so simple—and yet so impossible. I was never away from my cabin for any length of time, and the portmanteau was never left unlocked. I have the key here now.” He drew a small, oddly shaped key from his pocket and held it out for Poirot to see. “The lock was a special one, as Esmée told you, and I can swear that the key never left my person for a single moment.”

“It is very kind of you,” said Ridgeway, though his smile was a little weary. “But I fear the police have already done everything possible. They have been most thorough—and most fruitless. It is a nightmare, Monsieur Poirot. One moment the bonds are there, and the next—pouf! They are gone, and my reputation with them. My uncle is—well, he is a man of the old school. He does not say much, but I can see he thinks me a fool, or worse.”

“It is the mystery of the closed room, or rather, the closed box,” Poirot remarked, as he began to dismantle a piece of cheese with surgical precision. “Tell me, Monsieur Ridgeway, about the keys. There were, I understand, only three in existence?”

“That is so,” Philip answered. “One was held by Mr. Vavasour, one by Mr. Shaw, and the third was given to me. I never let it out of my possession. Even when I went to the baths, I took the precaution of locking my cabin door and keeping the key on its cord around my neck. It seems impossible, and yet the thing happened. On the last morning, just before we docked, I opened the trunk to find the package gone. The bonds had been replaced by a wad of heavy, worthless paper, and the wax seals of the Bank had been ruthlessly broken.”

“So you took care to be on the safe side,” he observed, with a
smile. “I hope Monsieur Poirot will be able to throw some light on
this extraordinary puzzle, for I confess frankly that I am nearly
out of my mind with worry and anxiety about it.”

Indeed, his face looked drawn and haggard and showed only too
clearly the strain under which he was labouring.

“Well, well,” said Poirot. “Let us lunch, and over lunch we will
put our heads together and see what can be done. I want to hear
Mr. Ridgeway’s story from his own lips.”

“The key, Mr. Ridgeway,” said Poirot, leaning forward and tapping the table with a precise finger. “That is the point of the greatest importance. How many keys were there to this special lock?” “Three,” replied the young man. “I had one, and the other two were held by the joint general managers—my uncle, Mr. Vavasour, and Mr. Shaw. They were the only three in existence, or so we were assured by the makers.” “And your key, it was with you always?” “It never left me. I carried it on a chain during the day, and at night it was tucked safely under my pillow.”

“How many keys were there to this trunk?” asked Poirot. Ridgeway explained that there were three in total: one which he carried on a chain about his person at all times, and two others which remained in the possession of the bank’s joint managers, Mr. Vavasour and Mr. Shaw. He admitted that he had left his cabin for meals and occasional exercise on deck, but emphasized that the trunk was always locked and that he had never parted with the key for a single second, though the scratches on the lock suggested a desperate, if ultimately unsuccessful, attempt to pick it before the thief had eventually found a way to turn the bolt.

“You had the key of the trunk on you, Mr. Ridgeway?” Poirot asked, his eyes narrowing slightly. “Always?”
“Always,” the young man replied. “It never left my person. I wore it on a chain around my neck. There were only three keys in existence, you see. Mine, and the two kept by the joint general managers at the Bank. Mr. Vavasour’s was in the safe, and Mr. Shaw had his at home—he had been away from the office for a few days with a severe chill. So, you see, it was impossible for anyone to have obtained a key unless they had robbed one of us three.”

“And the key?” inquired Poirot. “You had it always on your person?”
“I carried it in my pocket during the day, and at night it was under my pillow,” Ridgeway explained. “There were only three keys to that special lock. One, as I say, was with me; the other two were held by the joint general managers at the Bank—Mr. Vavasour and Mr. Shaw. They were kept in the Bank’s safe.”
“So that unless one of those two gentlemen is a thief, or you yourself, _mon ami_, the thing is an impossibility!” Poirot smiled, but his eyes were keen.

“But the key, Mr. Ridgeway, you had it with you?” Poirot’s eyes were sharp.

“Always. On a chain around my neck,” Ridgeway replied. “There are only three such keys in existence. I had one, and the other two were held by Mr. Vavasour and Mr. Shaw at the bank. It is quite impossible that anyone could have obtained them.”

Poirot nodded thoughtfully. “And yet, the lock was not forced in the end. It was turned. Tell me, when was the last time you saw the bonds intact?”

“Curious,” said Poirot, his eyes beginning to flicker with the
green light I knew so well. “Very curious! They waste much, much
time trying to prise it open, and then—_sapristi!_ they find that
they have the key all the time—for each of Hubbs’s locks are
unique.”

“That’s just why they couldn’t have had the key. It never left me
day or night.”

“You are sure of that?”

“I can swear to it, and besides, if they had had the key or a
duplicate, why should they waste time trying to force an obviously
unforceable lock?”

“They did. To hide them on the person would have been quite
impossible.”

“Then,” said Poirot, “it seems that they must have been—concealed
on the ship.”

“But the whole ship was searched!”

“The whole ship? That is a big thing, _mon ami_! Let us examine
this search. Who made it?”

“The Captain, the officers, and several of the stewards. They
went through every cabin, every hole and corner from stem to stern.”

“And they found—nothing?”

“Nothing.”

“Then,” said Poirot, “they must have been—overboard!”

“But they were sold in New York half an hour after we docked!”

“Quite so. Then they were not overboard. My friend, it is a
paradox! The bonds were not on the ship, they were not on the
people who left the ship, and yet they were in New York! It is
delightful!”

“It’s anything but delightful for me,” said Philip Ridgeway.

“I was speaking from the point of view of the problem,” apologized
Poirot. “But I can assure you that we will find the solution.”

“Oh, yes. I don’t say it was impossible to hide them on the person,
but it was very nearly so. In any case, as I say, every person
leaving the ship was searched.”

“I see. So we have this fact: the bonds were stolen between the
time you left the cabin after lunch and the time you returned to
it late in the afternoon. Now, who were the people who knew that
you had those bonds?”

“No one, so far as I am aware, except my uncle, Mr. Vavasour, and
Mr. Shaw.”

“And you think that one of them may have let the secret slip?”

“I don’t know what to think. Uncle is the soul of discretion,
and Mr. Shaw, too, I should have thought.”

“Who is this Mr. Shaw?”

“The other joint general manager. He has been with the Bank for
years—a very quiet, retiring man. He was out of the office for
some time before I sailed, through ill-health.”

“They did. They couldn’t have been concealed about anyone’s
person, and a search of the cabins and every possible corner of
the ship yielded no results. How then did they leave the ship?”

“How, indeed!” said Poirot. “By the way, did you have the same
cabin as on your previous trips?”

“No. I’ve always had a different one. This time it was 58 on B
deck.”

“And who was next door to you?”

“A very pleasant fellow, as a matter of fact. He’d crossed before
and we’d played bridge together. I found his name on the passenger
list—a Mr. Shaw, one of the joint general managers of the Bank.”

“Mr. Shaw?” Poirot looked at him with interest. “Did you see much
of him?”

“Oh, yes, we had several meals together.”

“And did he know about the bonds?”

“I suppose he must have. He’d probably have been in on it at the
Bank, though he didn’t mention them to me.”

“About the size of a five-pound note, only much thicker. You
couldn’t have missed them.”

“Then the thief must have disposed of them before he reached the
land. How?”

“Well, you know the way they were sold, Monsieur Poirot? Within
half an hour of the docking of the _Olympia_?”

“I do. It was that that struck me from the first as being most
significant. Half an hour! It is incredible! Only a man who was
waiting for them could have done it.”

“Exactly,” said Ridgeway. “But how did they get to him?”

“That is what we have to find out. Tell me, did you see anyone
leaving the ship with a particularly large cigar or anything of
that sort? No? You shake your head. Well, well.”

Poirot fell into a brown study.

“There are two people,” he said at last, “who could have done it.
One of them must have done it. One is the thief, and the other is—?”

He stopped.

“The other is who, Monsieur Poirot?” asked Miss Farquhar.

“The man who received the bonds,” said Poirot. “Now let us see.”

He sat in silence for some minutes. Then he looked up at me.

“Hastings, my friend, what do you say to it?”

“Well,” I said, “it seems to me that the thief must have been someone
on board who was in communication with someone on land. The bonds
were probably passed to the receiver by some means or other, but
how, I can’t imagine.”

“No,” said Poirot. “That’s the difficulty. But let us consider the
facts. The bonds were in the trunk, and the trunk was locked. The
lock was a special one, and the key never left Mr. Ridgeway’s
possession. Yet the bonds were stolen. How?”

“By someone who had a duplicate key,” I suggested.

“But Hubbs’s locks are unique,” said Poirot. “No two are alike.”

“Then it must have been someone who picked the lock,” I said.

“But the lock was not picked,” said Poirot. “It was opened with a
key.”

“How do you know that?” I asked.

“Because if it had been picked, it would have been damaged,” said
Poirot. “And Mr. Ridgeway says it was not damaged.”

“Then how was it opened?” I asked.

“That is what we have to find out,” said Poirot. “But let us consider
another possibility. Suppose the bonds were not in the trunk at
all?”

“Not in the trunk!” cried Ridgeway. “But I put them there myself!”

“I know you did,” said Poirot. “But suppose someone took them out
before you locked the trunk?”

“But I locked the trunk immediately,” said Ridgeway.

“I know you did,” said Poirot. “But suppose someone took them out
between the time you put them in and the time you locked the trunk?”

“But I was there all the time!” said Ridgeway.

“I know you were,” said Poirot. “But suppose someone took them out
while you were not looking?”

“But I was looking!” said Ridgeway.

“I know you were,” said Poirot. “But suppose someone took them out
without you seeing them?”

“But how could they?” said Ridgeway.

“That is what we have to find out,” said Poirot. “But let us consider
yet another possibility. Suppose the bonds were not stolen at all?”

“Not stolen!” cried Ridgeway. “But they’re gone!”

“I know they’re gone,” said Poirot. “But suppose they were not
stolen?”

“Then what happened to them?” asked Ridgeway.

“That is what we have to find out,” said Poirot. “But let us consider
one more possibility. Suppose the bonds were never in the trunk at
all?”

“Never in the trunk!” cried Ridgeway. “But I saw them put there!”

“I know you did,” said Poirot. “But suppose what you saw put there
were not the bonds at all?”

“Not the bonds!” cried Ridgeway. “But what else could they have
been?”

“That is what we have to find out,” said Poirot. “And I think I know
how to find it out. Mr. Ridgeway, I should like to see that trunk.”

“Certainly,” said Ridgeway. “It’s at my rooms. I’ll take you there
now.”

We all drove to Ridgeway’s rooms, and he showed us the trunk. It
was a large, heavy cabin trunk, with a special Hubbs’s lock. Poirot
examined it carefully.

“It has certainly been scratched and cut about,” he said. “But as
you say, the lock itself is undamaged. And you are sure you had
the only key?”

“Quite sure,” said Ridgeway.

“And you never let it out of your possession?”

“Never.”

“Not even for a moment?”

“Not even for a moment.”

“And you were with the trunk all the time it was in your cabin?”

“Yes.”

“And you never left the cabin while the trunk was there?”

“Well, I went to meals, of course.”

“And you locked the cabin door when you went to meals?”

“Yes.”

“And you had the only key to the cabin door?”

“No, the steward had a key, of course.”

“Aha!” said Poirot. “The steward! Now we are getting somewhere.
Who was the steward?”

“A man named Smith,” said Ridgeway. “He’s been with the company
for years. A very reliable man, I believe.”

“We shall see,” said Poirot. “And now, Mr. Ridgeway, I should like
to see the place where the bonds were handed over to you.”

“That was at the Bank,” said Ridgeway. “In the manager’s room.”

“And who was present?”

“Mr. Vavasour and Mr. Shaw.”

“And they both saw the bonds put into the package?”

“Yes.”

“And they both saw the package put into the trunk?”

“Yes.”

“And they both saw you lock the trunk?”

“Yes.”

“And they both saw you take the key?”

“Yes.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “Well, Mr. Ridgeway, I think I have all the
information I need for the moment. I will let you know if I
discover anything.”

We left Ridgeway’s rooms and walked back to Poirot’s flat.

“Well, Poirot,” I said, “what do you think of it?”

“It is a very interesting case, Hastings,” he said. “A very
interesting case indeed.”

“Do you think the steward did it?” I asked.

“The steward?” said Poirot. “No, I do not think the steward did
it. He would have had to have a duplicate key to the trunk, and we
know that Hubbs’s locks are unique.”

“Then who do you think did it?” I asked.

“I do not know yet,” said Poirot. “But I have a little idea. A
very little idea.”

He would say no more, and for the next few days he was very busy.
He went to the Bank and interviewed Mr. Vavasour and Mr. Shaw. He
went to the Docks and interviewed the Customs authorities. He even
went to Liverpool and interviewed the people who had fitted the
lock to the trunk.

And then, one morning, he came into the room with a smile on his
face.

“Hastings,” he said, “I have found the thief.”

“The thief!” I cried. “Who is it?”

“Wait a moment, my friend,” he said. “First we must assemble the
suspects.”

He sent off several telegrams, and a few hours later, Mr. Vavasour,
Mr. Shaw, Philip Ridgeway and Miss Farquhar were all assembled in
our room.

“Messieurs, Mademoiselle,” said Poirot, “I have asked you here
because I have discovered the truth about the disappearance of the
Liberty Bonds.”

There was a moment of tense silence. Everyone looked at Poirot.

“The problem,” he continued, “was a very simple one, once one
realized the significance of certain facts. The bonds were in a
locked trunk, to which there was only one key. That key was in the
possession of Mr. Ridgeway. Yet the bonds were stolen. How?”

He paused.

“The answer,” he said, “is that they were not stolen from the trunk
at all.”

“Not stolen from the trunk!” cried Ridgeway. “But I saw them put
there!”

“You saw a package put there,” said Poirot. “But that package did
not contain the bonds.”

“Not contain the bonds!” cried Ridgeway. “But I saw them put in!”

“You saw them put into a package,” said Poirot. “But you did not
see that package put into the trunk.”

“But I did!” said Ridgeway.

“No,” said Poirot. “What you saw put into the trunk was another
package, identical in appearance to the first one.”

“But how could that be?” asked Ridgeway.

“It was very simple,” said Poirot. “While you were momentarily
distracted, the packages were switched.”

“But who could have done it?” asked Ridgeway.

“Only someone who was present when the bonds were packed,” said
Poirot. “And that means either Mr. Vavasour or Mr. Shaw.”

Everyone looked at the two managers. Mr. Vavasour looked indignant,
while Mr. Shaw looked merely surprised.

“But which of them was it?” I asked.

“That,” said Poirot, “was the question I had to answer. And the
answer was provided by the fact that the bonds were sold in New
York within half an hour of the docking of the _Olympia_.”

“But how does that help?” I asked.

“Because,” said Poirot, “it means that the thief must have been in
New York at the time.”

“But neither Mr. Vavasour nor Mr. Shaw were in New York,” I said.

“One of them was,” said Poirot. “Mr. Shaw.”

“Mr. Shaw!” I cried. “But he was here in London!”

“Was he?” said Poirot. “He was away from the Bank for several days
on account of illness, was he not?”

“Yes,” said Mr. Vavasour. “He had a very bad attack of bronchitis.”

“A very convenient attack of bronchitis,” said Poirot. “It allowed
him to travel to New York on a faster ship—the _Gigantic_—which
arrived several hours before the _Olympia_.”

“But this is preposterous!” cried Mr. Shaw. “I was in bed all the
time!”

“Were you?” said Poirot. “I think not. I think you were in New
York, waiting for the _Olympia_ to dock. And when she did, you
simply collected the bonds from the person you had arranged to
meet.”

“And who was that person?” I asked.

“That,” said Poirot, “is the most clever part of the whole plot.
The person who brought the bonds to New York was none other than—
Mr. Ridgeway himself!”

“Mr. Ridgeway!” I cried.

“Yes,” said Poirot. “But he did not know he was doing it. You see,
the package he put in his trunk did not contain the bonds. But the
package he carried in his pocket did!”

“In his pocket!” cried Ridgeway.

“Yes,” said Poirot. “Do you remember, Mr. Ridgeway, that just
before you left the Bank, Mr. Shaw gave you a small package of
papers to deliver to the Bank’s New York agents?”

“Yes,” said Ridgeway. “I remember.”

“Well,” said Poirot, “that package contained the Liberty Bonds.
And while you were guarding your trunk with such care, the bonds
were safely in your pocket all the time!”

“But why the business with the trunk?” I asked.

“To provide an explanation for the disappearance of the bonds,”
said Poirot. “Mr. Shaw knew that the trunk would be searched, and
he provided the evidence of an attempted robbery to make it look
as though the bonds had been stolen from it. It was a very clever
plan, but it had one fatal flaw.”

“And what was that?” I asked.

“The time,” said Poirot. “If the bonds had been stolen from the
trunk, they could not have been sold in New York within half an
hour of the ship’s arrival. It would have taken much longer than
that for the thief to get ashore and find a buyer. But if the bonds
were already in New York, in the hands of someone who was waiting
for them—well, then it was a different matter entirely.”

Mr. Shaw made a sudden movement towards the door, but Poirot was
too quick for him.

“No, no, Mr. Shaw,” he said. “It is no use. The police are waiting
outside.”

And indeed, at that moment, two plain-clothes officers entered the
room and led the unfortunate Mr. Shaw away.

“Well, Poirot,” I said, when they had gone, “that was a very
clever piece of work.”

“It was a very interesting case, Hastings,” he said. “A very
interesting case indeed. But now, if you will excuse me, I think I
will have a little nap. All this excitement has made me quite
fatigued.”

And with that, he settled himself comfortably in his armchair and
closed his eyes.

“About the size of a large cigar box,” said Ridgeway. “You see,
each bond was for five hundred dollars, and there were two thousand
of them.”

“Then it was impossible for any one to have had them on his person?”

“Quite. And since they have not been found on board——”

“It is all very remarkable,” said Poirot. “There was a thorough
search, I suppose?”

“A very thorough search. The captain, I must say, was most kind.”

“And you were present, of course?”

“Yes, I accompanied the searchers. It was quite a long business.”

“And what about the other passengers?”

“They were all most helpful. There was no one who could possibly
be suspected. Most of them were American business men, and there
were one or two quite well-known people—Mr. Shaw, for instance.”

“Ah! was Mr. Shaw on board?”

“Oh, didn’t you know? He had been ordered a sea voyage for his
health. He had a touch of bronchitis, I believe.”

“And Mr. Vavasour? He did not go also?”

“Oh, no, he was in London. But I wish he’d been there! He’s a
terrible old martinet, and he’s everlastingly on to me about the
whole thing. He says I was careless—that I must have talked.”

“And did you?”

“Not a word to a soul. I knew the responsibility I had on my
shoulders. I didn’t even tell Esmée here.”

Miss Farquhar nodded.

“That is quite true,” she said. “I had no idea Philip was taking the
bonds.”

“Well, it’s a very pretty problem,” said Poirot, “and I shall
be delighted to see what I can do. I think I’ll go and have a look
at the _Olympia_ herself. She’s at Liverpool now, I believe?”

“Yes, she arrived there yesterday.”

“Then we will go to Liverpool. Hastings, you will come with me?”

I agreed, and we started off that afternoon.

“Certainly they did. They could hardly have been hidden on board—and
anyway we know they weren’t because they were offered for sale
within half an hour of the _Olympia’s_ arrival, long before I got
the cables going and the numbers sent out. One broker swears he
bought some of them even before the _Olympia_ got in. But you can’t
send bonds by wireless.”

“Not by wireless, but did any tug come alongside?”

We drove at once to the City and were soon ushered into the private room of Mr. Vavasour. He was a man of about fifty, of an almost daunting respectability, with a high, balding forehead and gold-rimmed pince-nez. He greeted us with a stiff courtesy and looked with some interest at his nephew’s card which Poirot handed him.

We thanked our new friends and took our leave. The London and Scottish Bank was an imposing building in the heart of the City, and we were soon ushered into the private room of Mr. Vavasour. He was a man of the old school, tall and dignified, with a somewhat stiff manner. He read his nephew’s card, then looked at us over his gold-rimmed spectacles with a mixture of curiosity and reserve.

We took our leave of the two young people and drove straight to the City. The London and Scottish Bank was an imposing edifice, and the name of Mr. Vavasour acted like a magic password that admitted us to the inner sanctum. Mr. Vavasour was a man of weight and substance, the very image of a responsible banker. With him was a man of a different stamp, thinner and looking somewhat ill, whom he introduced as his colleague, Mr. Shaw.

The London and Scottish Bank was an imposing edifice, and the name of Mr. Vavasour proved a sufficient introduction to its inner sanctum. We were shown into a large, sombre room where two men awaited us. Mr. Vavasour was a tall, elderly man of distinguished appearance, whose face bore the marks of recent anxiety. His colleague, Mr. Shaw, was a man of a different type—slightly younger, with a keen, energetic face and a pair of very shrewd eyes. It was Mr. Vavasour who spoke first, his voice heavy with the gravity of the situation.

We found the London and Scottish Bank to be an imposing edifice in the City. On presenting Philip Ridgeway’s card, we were shown at once into the private room of Mr. Vavasour. He was a man of grave and dignified appearance, the very soul of banking respectability. He read his nephew’s note and sighed heavily, looking at us over the top of his gold-rimmed pince-nez. “A most distressing business, Monsieur Poirot,” he remarked. “Distressing for the Bank, and even more so for my nephew. I have always had the highest opinion of Philip’s integrity, but I cannot deny that his conduct in this matter seems to have been—shall we say, somewhat negligent? My colleague, Mr. Shaw, is even more perturbed than I am; unfortunately, he is at present confined to his house with a severe attack of bronchitis, or he would have been here to discuss the matter with you.”

Poirot thanked him, bade farewell to Miss Farquhar, and together
we started out for Threadneedle Street and the head office of the
London and Scottish Bank. On production of Ridgeway’s card, we were
led through the labyrinth of counters and desks, skirting paying-in
clerks and paying-out clerks and up to a small office on the first
floor where the joint general managers received us. They were two
grave gentlemen, who had grown grey in the service of the Bank.
Mr. Vavasour had a short white beard, Mr. Shaw was clean shaven.

“It is a most distressing business, Monsieur Poirot,” said Mr. Vavasour, as we seated ourselves. “A terrible blow to the Bank. And for my nephew, it is a tragedy. I have always had the highest opinion of Philip.” Poirot nodded sympathetically. “Quite so, quite so. Now, messieurs, let us go back to the morning of the 23rd. You handed the bonds over to Mr. Ridgeway?” “We did,” replied Mr. Shaw. “We counted them together—a million dollars in Liberty Bonds. They were then placed in the leather case, and the case itself was put into the portmanteau, which we then saw Mr. Ridgeway lock with his own key.”

“It is a most lamentable affair,” began Mr. Vavasour, sighing heavily. “A terrible blow to the prestige of an institution such as ours. My nephew, I am sure—”
“Is a young man of the highest integrity,” interrupted Mr. Shaw. He coughed, a dry, hacking sound. “We do not suspect him, Monsieur Poirot, but the disappearance of the bonds remains a mystery that the police have been unable to solve. They were sealed in this very room, placed in the portmanteau, and the lock—a masterpiece of Hubbs’s—was fastened.”

“It is a most lamentable affair,” began Mr. Vavasour, after Poirot had explained the nature of our visit. “My nephew is a young man of whom I have always had the highest opinion, but I fear he has been—well, perhaps a little indiscreet. He may have talked too much on the voyage.” Mr. Shaw, who appeared to be suffering from a severe cold, nodded his head in agreement. “Quite so, quite so,” he wheezed. “A million dollars is a great temptation, and there are many light-fingered gentry on these large liners who are always on the look-out for such a chance. We did our best to safeguard the Bank’s interests. The bonds were counted and sealed in the presence of us both, and we saw them safely locked into the portmanteau.”

“It is a most deplorable affair,” said Mr. Vavasour, shaking his head. “The loss is heavy, but the blow to our prestige is heavier. We have always reposed the utmost confidence in my nephew.” Mr. Shaw nodded in agreement. “We were both present when the bonds were packed,” he explained in a thin, somewhat strained voice. “I myself had insisted upon the special Hubbs’s lock for the portmanteau. We saw the bonds counted and placed within, and the package was then sealed with the Bank’s seal before Philip locked the trunk.”

“We understand you wish to inquire into the details of this unfortunate occurrence,” said Mr. Vavasour, after we had seated ourselves. “It is a most distressing affair. My nephew, I fear, has been—at the very least—extremely careless. The Bank’s reputation is at stake, and we are naturally anxious to clear the matter up as quickly as possible.”

“I understand you are strictly a private inquiry agent?” said Mr.
Vavasour. “Quite so, quite so. We have, of course, placed ourselves
in the hands of Scotland Yard. Inspector McNeil has charge of the
case. A very able officer, I believe.”

“I am sure of it,” said Poirot politely. “You will permit a few
questions, on your nephew’s behalf? About this lock, who ordered
it from Hubbs’s?”

“I ordered it myself,” said Mr. Shaw. “I would not trust to any
clerk in the matter. As to the keys, Mr. Ridgeway had one, and the
other two are held by my colleague and myself.”

“And no clerk has had access to them?”

“Most certainly not,” replied Mr. Vavasour with some asperity. “My own key has never left my person; it is attached to my watch-chain. As for Mr. Shaw’s key, I believe he kept it in a small safe at his private residence.” Mr. Shaw nodded in agreement. “That is so,” he added. “It was never out of my possession for a single moment. The idea of a duplicate being made is, I assure you, quite out of the question.”

“Absolutely not,” Mr. Vavasour replied with some starchiness. “The keys have remained in our respective private safes, to which only we have the combinations. The package was sealed in our presence, and Philip placed it directly into the portmanteau. We then saw him lock it with his own key before he departed for Liverpool. It was a most straightforward procedure, Monsieur Poirot, and it is quite inconceivable how any substitution could have taken place at this end.”

“Certainly not,” replied Mr. Vavasour. “My own key has not left my possession since it was delivered to me, and Mr. Shaw’s is kept in the bank’s private safe, the combination of which is known only to the two of us. It is quite impossible that any unauthorized person could have obtained either of them. As for the package itself, it was sealed in our presence and handed to Philip immediately before he left for the station. There was no opportunity for it to be tampered with here.”

“None,” said Mr. Vavasour. “They have been kept in our respective
private safes, and I think I can say that they have never been out
of our personal possession.” Poirot nodded. “And the bonds
themselves? They were, I understand, in your joint possession until
the morning of the twenty-third?” “Precisely,” replied Mr. Shaw.
“They were brought from the strong room, counted in our presence,
and then placed in the package which was sealed with the Bank’s
seal.”

“None,” replied Mr. Vavasour. “They are kept in our private safes, to which no one but ourselves has access. Even the duplicates provided by the makers were delivered directly into our hands.” Poirot nodded thoughtfully. “And these safes, they were not tampered with, I suppose? No, that would be too much to hope for. But tell me, during the period when the bonds were being prepared, did any other person—perhaps a trusted subordinate—have the opportunity to handle the package?” Mr. Shaw shook his head decisively. “The bonds were counted by us personally, placed in the case, and the case was sealed by us both in the presence of my nephew. From that moment until he reached the ship, the package never left his sight.”

Mr. Shaw turned inquiringly to Mr. Vavasour. “I think I am correct
in saying that they have remained in the safe where we placed them
on the 23rd,” said Mr. Vavasour. “My colleague was unfortunately
taken ill a fortnight ago—in fact on the very day that Philip left
us. He has only just recovered.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “And where is this safe?”

“In the next room, Monsieur Poirot,” said Mr. Shaw, rising. “I
will show it to you. It is a very large one, and as you will see,
the lock is a most complicated one.”

Poirot inspected the safe with great interest, and we then took
our leave of the two bank managers.

“Well, what do you think of it, Poirot?” I asked when we were once
more in the street.

“My friend, I think it is a very interesting case. I see light, a
very small ray of light, in the distance.”

“But how could the bonds have been stolen?”

“Ah! how? that is the question. The portmanteau is locked, and the
only two other keys are in the safe of the London and Scottish
Bank. Then the bonds are stolen on board the _Olympia_? No,
Hastings, I do not believe they were.”

“You mean they were never in the portmanteau at all?”

“Exactly.”

“But Mr. Ridgeway saw them put in!”

“Yes, he saw a package, Hastings, which he thought contained the
bonds. He never saw the bonds themselves. But we shall see, we
shall see.”

“What are you going to do now?”

“I have several things to do, but I shall begin by calling on Mr.
Shaw’s doctor. I think he will be able to tell me something
interesting.”

“But why his doctor?”

“Wait and see, my friend, wait and see.”

Poirot’s inquiries at the doctor’s were soon over. We then went
to a small hotel in the West End where we found Philip Ridgeway
and Miss Farquhar waiting for us. They were both looking very
anxious.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot,” said Miss Farquhar, “have you found out
anything?”

“I have found out several things, mademoiselle,” said Poirot
gravely. “And I think I can promise you that the thief will be
in custody before long.”

“Then you know who it is?” cried Philip Ridgeway.

“I have a very good idea, but I must be sure before I make an
accusation. Now I must ask you both to come with me to the London
and Scottish Bank. I have something to say to Mr. Vavasour and Mr.
Shaw.”

When we arrived at the Bank, we were at once shown into the room
where we had seen the two managers before. They both looked very
surprised to see us.

“I have come to tell you, gentlemen,” said Poirot, “that I have
discovered who stole the Liberty Bonds.”

“What!” cried Mr. Vavasour. “You don’t mean to say so?”

“Yes, and I will tell you how it was done. It was a very clever
plot, but there was one small detail which the thief forgot.”

“And what was that?” asked Mr. Shaw.

“He forgot that I, Hercule Poirot, might be called in to
investigate the case!” said Poirot with a smile. “Now, Mr.
Ridgeway, will you be so good as to tell us exactly what happened
when you saw the bonds placed in the portmanteau?”

“Well,” said Philip Ridgeway, “Mr. Vavasour and Mr. Shaw were both
there. Mr. Shaw had the bonds in his hand, and he counted them over
before me. Then he put them into the package and sealed it with
the bank’s seal. Then I put the package into the portmanteau and
locked it.”

“And you are quite sure that it was the package containing the
bonds that you put into the portmanteau?”

“Of course I am! I saw them put in!”

“Ah! but did you see them put into the package?”

“Yes, I did.”

“And was the package out of your sight for a single moment after
it had been sealed?”

“No, not for a second.”

“Then,” said Poirot, “the thief must be someone who had access to
the portmanteau after it was locked. And there are only two people
who could have had a key—Mr. Vavasour and Mr. Shaw.”

“But the keys were in the safe!” cried Mr. Vavasour.

“Were they?” said Poirot. “Mr. Shaw, you were taken ill on the
very day that Mr. Ridgeway left for New York. What was the matter
with you?”

“I had a very severe attack of bronchitis,” said Mr. Shaw. “I was
in bed for a fortnight.”

“And did you see a doctor?”

“Of course I did.”

“And what did he say?”

“He said I must stay in bed and take great care of myself.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “And did you have a nurse?”

“No, my wife looked after me.”

“I see. And where were the keys of the safe during your illness?”

“They were in my pocket, of course.”

“And did anyone else have access to your clothes?”

“No one but my wife.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “Well, Mr. Vavasour, I think I can tell you
who stole the bonds. It was Mr. Shaw!”

“What!” cried Mr. Vavasour. “Shaw! It’s impossible!”

“Not at all,” said Poirot. “It was very simple. Mr. Shaw did not
have bronchitis at all. He only pretended to be ill so that he
could go to New York on the _Olympia_ and steal the bonds!”

“But he was here all the time!” cried Mr. Vavasour.

“No, he wasn't,” said Poirot. “He went to Liverpool and got on the
_Olympia_ under an assumed name. He had a duplicate key to the
portmanteau, and he stole the bonds and sold them in New York. Then
he came back to London and pretended to have recovered from his
illness.”

“But this is preposterous!” cried Mr. Shaw. “I have never been to
New York in my life!”

“Oh, yes, you have,” said Poirot. “I have been to see your doctor,
and he tells me that he did not see you at all during your illness.
He only spoke to your wife on the telephone, and she told him that
you were too ill to see him!”

“Is this true, Shaw?” asked Mr. Vavasour.

Mr. Shaw did not answer. He turned very pale and sank into a chair.

“It is true,” he whispered. “I did it. I was in debt, and I saw
a way to get the money. I’m sorry, Vavasour, I’m sorry.”

“And what about the bonds?” asked Mr. Vavasour.

“I sold them all,” said Mr. Shaw. “The money is gone.”

“Well, Mr. Shaw,” said Poirot, “I’m afraid you will have to
answer for your crime. I have already informed the police, and
they are on their way here now.”

And indeed, at 그 moment, Inspector McNeil entered the room with
two other officers.

“Mr. Shaw,” he said, “I am arresting you for the theft of a
million dollars’ worth of Liberty Bonds. Anything you say may be
used in evidence against you.”

As Mr. Shaw was led away, Mr. Vavasour turned to Poirot.

“Monsieur Poirot,” he said, “I don’t know how to thank you. You
have saved the reputation of the Bank, and you have cleared my
nephew’s name.”

“It was nothing, Monsieur Vavasour,” said Poirot. “A very simple
little problem. But it just shows that even the cleverest criminal
can make a mistake.”

And with a bow, Poirot led us out of the room.

“Well, Poirot,” I said, as we walked back to our rooms, “that was
a very clever bit of work. How did you know that it was Mr. Shaw?”

“My friend,” said Poirot, “it was the lock. You remember what Mr.
Ridgeway said? The thief tried to force the lock, but couldn’t.
Then he must have had a key. And who had a key? Only Mr. Vavasour
and Mr. Shaw. And as Mr. Shaw was conveniently ill at the time,
it was obvious that he was the one who had the opportunity.”

“But how did you know he wasn’t really ill?”

“Because, my friend, I went to see his doctor! And when he told
me that he hadn’t actually seen Mr. Shaw, I knew that I was on the
right track. It was a very clever plot, but as I said, there was
one small detail that the thief forgot.”

“And what was that?”

“He forgot that Hercule Poirot has a very good memory for faces!
I saw him on the _Olympia_ myself, though he didn't see me!”

“But Poirot,” I said, “you said you hadn’t been on the _Olympia_!”

“Ah! that was a little white lie, Hastings! To catch a thief, one
must sometimes be a little bit of a thief oneself!”

And Poirot laughed his quiet, inward laugh.

“Ah!” cried Poirot. “How very inconvenient! And you, monsieur, you
have had no ill health? You have not been away from your work?”

“I have not been away for a single day. I have been at my post
all the time, since Mr. Shaw’s illness threw a double burden on
my shoulders.”

Poirot appeared to be much struck by this.

“And you, monsieur,” he said, turning to Mr. Shaw. “You are quite
well again now?”

“I am much better, thank you,” said Mr. Shaw. “Though still a
little shaky.”

“And you were taken ill on the day that the bonds were sent?”

“Exactly.”

Poirot’s eyes flickered.

“The 23rd, was it not?”

“Yes, the 23rd.”

“_Tiens!_ that is very curious! And did you both see the bonds
counted and sealed into the package?”

“We did,” they replied together. “We were both present when it
was handed over to Mr. Ridgeway.”

“Then it seems to me that we must look for the thief on board the
_Olympia_,” said Poirot, with a little shrug of the shoulders.
“Good-day to you, gentlemen.”

We then bowed ourselves out of the room.

“Quite so, quite so. And you, Mr. Shaw, were you at the Bank that
morning?”

“Yes, I was here for a few hours. I went home early on account of
my cold.”

Poirot’s eyes flickered.

“And you were also present when the bonds were placed in the
portmanteau?”

“Yes, we both were.”

“The lock was a very good one, was it not?”

“Very. It was a special lock that I had made for the purpose.
The keys are different from any others of Hubbs’s manufacture.
They were most careful about it.”

“I see. Now, Mr. Shaw, can you tell me exactly when you last saw
the bonds?”

“I saw them placed in the trunk, as I told you.”

“And you, Mr. Vavasour?”

“I also saw them placed in the trunk.”

“And then?”

“The trunk was locked and the key handed to Philip.”

“And what did he do with it?”

“He put it in his pocket.”

“And then?”

“He left the office with the trunk.”

“And you both saw him go?”

“Yes.”

“And no one else was present?”

“No one.”

“Thank you, gentlemen. That is all I have to ask.”

We were escorted to the door by a very polite clerk.

“Ah! so he was not here on the day the bonds were stolen?” Poirot’s
eyes were fixed on Mr. Shaw, who seemed slightly confused.

“No, I was at home, nursing a very sharp attack of bronchitis.
A most unfortunate illness.”

“And you, Mr. Vavasour, you were here?”

“Oh, yes, and I can assure you that everything was done with the
utmost care. The bonds were counted, packed, and sealed in the
presence of my colleague and myself. Then they were handed to Philip,
and he locked them in the portmanteau. It was then half-past ten,
and he was to leave for Liverpool at once.”

“And since then?”

“Since then, nothing has been seen of them. They have been sold
in New York, as you know.”

“By whom?”

“A small firm of brokers. They refuse to give any information,
beyond the fact that they bought the bonds from a young man who
looked like a clerk.”

Poirot’s eyes had a far-away look in them.

“I see,” he murmured. “And this young man, was he at all like
Mr. Philip Ridgeway?”

“The description might apply to him, certainly,” said Mr. Vavasour.
“But it might also apply to any young man of his age.”

“And now, Mr. Vavasour,” said Poirot, rising, “I will bid you
good-afternoon. There is just one more question I should like to
ask—is there any one in the Bank who was particularly anxious to
go to America instead of your nephew?”

Mr. Vavasour thought for a moment.

“There were several applicants, of course. But none that we
seriously considered. My nephew is well known in New York, and it
was for that reason we selected him.”

“Thank you,” said Poirot. “And now, I wish you a very good day.”

We walked down to the street in silence.

“Well, what do you think of it?” I asked, when we reached the
pavement.

“My friend,” said Poirot, “it is a very interesting case. Very
interesting indeed. One of the most interesting I have ever had
the honour of investigating.”

“But it seems so simple!” I cried. “The bonds were stolen on the
boat, and sold in New York.”

“Ah!” said Poirot. “And how were they sold in New York before the
boat arrived? That is the question, my friend. That is the
question.”

“Perhaps there was a confederate in New York?” I suggested.

“No, that would not do. The bonds were sold within half an hour
of the _Olympia’s_ arrival. That means they must have been on
the boat. And yet they were sold before the boat arrived. It is a
paradox, my friend. A paradox!”

“But how could they be sold before the boat arrived?” I persisted.

“That,” said Poirot, “is what we have to find out.”

He took a taxi and we drove back to our rooms.

“And now,” said Poirot, when we were once more settled in our
arm-chairs, “let us review the facts of the case. The bonds were
stolen from a trunk which had been specially fitted with a Hubbs’s
lock. The thief first tried to force the lock, and then, finding
he could not do so, used a key. Now, where did he get that key?”

“He might have had a duplicate made?” I suggested.

“No, that is impossible. Hubbs’s locks are unique. No two are
alike. There were only three keys in existence. One was held by
Philip Ridgeway, one by Mr. Vavasour, and one by Mr. Shaw.”

“Then one of them must have been the thief!” I cried.

“Not necessarily,” said Poirot. “There is another possibility.”

“What is that?”

“That the bonds were never in the trunk at all!”

“But Philip Ridgeway saw them put in!”

“He saw a package put in. He did not see what was in the package.”

“But Mr. Vavasour and Mr. Shaw saw them put in!”

“They saw them put in a package. They did not see the package put
in the trunk.”

“But Philip Ridgeway says he saw it!”

“He saw a package. It might not have been the same one.”

“But who could have changed it?”

“That is the question, my friend. That is the question.”

He sat for some time in silence, his eyes closed, his brow furrowed
in thought. Then he rose and began to pace the room.

“Hastings,” he said, “I have an idea. A very strange idea. I must
go to the Bank again.”

“But we have only just come from there!”

“No matter. I must go again. There is something I must find out.”

He hurried out of the room, and I followed him. We reached the
Bank just as it was closing. Poirot asked for Mr. Vavasour, and
we were shown into his office.

“Mr. Vavasour,” said Poirot, “I have one more question to ask you.
On the morning the bonds were sent off, did you or Mr. Shaw leave
the room for any reason?”

Mr. Vavasour thought for a moment.

“Yes,” he said, “I remember now. Mr. Shaw was taken ill—the first
attack of his bronchitis. He had a violent fit of coughing, and
I went to get him a glass of water.”

“And how long were you away?”

“Oh, only a minute or two. Not more.”

“And was Philip Ridgeway in the room all the time?”

“Yes, he was waiting for the package.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “Thank you, Mr. Vavasour. That is all I
wanted to know.”

He turned and left the office, and I followed him.

“Well?” I said, when we were once more in the street. “What does
it mean?”

“It means, my friend, that the case is even more interesting than
I thought. Come, let us go and see Miss Farquhar.”

We found Miss Farquhar at her flat. She seemed surprised to see
us.

“Have you found out anything, Monsieur Poirot?” she asked
anxiously.

“I have found out a great deal, mademoiselle,” said Poirot. “But
there is one thing I should like to ask you. When you were at the
‘Cheshire Cheese’ this morning, did you notice anything peculiar
about Mr. Ridgeway’s appearance?”

Miss Farquhar looked puzzled.

“Peculiar? No, I don’t think so. He looked very tired and worried,
of course.”

“Nothing else? Think, mademoiselle. Think.”

She shook her head.

“No, I can’t remember anything.”

“Wait!” I cried. “I remember something! His hair! It was grey at
the temples!”

“Ah!” said Poirot. “And was it grey before he went to America?”

“No,” said Miss Farquhar. “I don’t think so. I noticed it this
morning for the first time. But I thought it was just the worry
and the anxiety.”

“Worry and anxiety do not turn a man’s hair grey in a week,” said
Poirot. “Not even a million dollars’ worth of worry and anxiety.
No, mademoiselle, there is another explanation.”

“What is it?” I asked.

“The explanation, my friend, is that the man we saw this morning
was not Philip Ridgeway!”

“Not Philip Ridgeway!” I cried. “But Miss Farquhar knew him!”

“She thought she knew him,” said Poirot. “But she had not seen him
for a week. And in that week he had grown a beard—no, he had
shaved off a beard—no, what am I saying? He had changed, my
friend. He had changed.”

“But why should he change?”

“To deceive us, Hastings. To deceive us.”

“But if he wasn’t Philip Ridgeway, who was he?”

“He was the man who stole the bonds!”

“But how could he steal the bonds if he wasn’t Philip Ridgeway?”

“That,” said Poirot, “is what I am going to find out. Come,
Hastings, we must go to the _Olympia_!”

We took the night train to Liverpool, and the next morning we were
on board the _Olympia_. Poirot spent the morning interviewing
the stewards and the officers. Then he went to the purser’s
office.

“Monsieur,” he said, “I am Hercule Poirot. I am investigating the
theft of the Liberty Bonds.”

The purser looked interested.

“Ah, yes,” he said. “A very mysterious business. Can I help you
in any way?”

“I should like to see the list of passengers,” said Poirot.

The purser handed it to him. Poirot scanned it quickly.

“Ah!” he said. “Here is the name I was looking for. Mr. Philip
Ridgeway. And here is another name—Mr. Guy Vavasour.”

“Mr. Vavasour?” I said. “The uncle?”

“No,” said Poirot. “Not the uncle. The nephew.”

“But Philip Ridgeway is the nephew!”

“There are two nephews, my friend. Two nephews.”

He turned to the purser.

“This Mr. Guy Vavasour—what was he like?”

“A tall, dark man,” said the purser. “Very quiet and reserved. He
kept to himself a good deal.”

“And Mr. Philip Ridgeway?”

“A young man, fair-haired, very pleasant and outgoing. He was
very popular on board.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “And did they know each other?”

“I don't think so. They were never seen together.”

“And did they both leave the ship at New York?”

“Yes.”

“Thank you,” said Poirot. “That is all I wanted to know.”

He turned to me.

“You see, Hastings? The plot thickens!”

“But I don’t understand!” I cried. “Who stole the bonds?”

“The man who stole the bonds,” said Poirot, “is the man we saw
this morning.”

“But who was he?”

“He was Mr. Guy Vavasour!”

“But Miss Farquhar said he was Philip Ridgeway!”

“She was deceived, my friend. Deceived by a resemblance—and by
something else.”

“What else?”

“That,” said Poirot, “is what I am going to show you.”

He led the way to the deck.

“Look, Hastings,” he said, pointing to a man who was sitting in
a deck-chair. “Do you see that man?”

I looked. It was the man we had seen at the ‘Cheshire Cheese’—the
man who called himself Philip Ridgeway.

“But what is he doing here?” I cried.

“He is waiting for us, my friend,” said Poirot. “He is waiting for
us.”

He walked up to the man.

“Mr. Guy Vavasour, I believe?”

The man looked up, his face pale and drawn.

“Yes,” he said. “I am Guy Vavasour.”

“And you stole the bonds?”

The man nodded.

“Yes,” he said. “I stole them.”

“But how?” I cried. “How did you do it?”

“It was simple enough,” said Vavasour. “I knew that Philip was
going to America with the bonds. I knew that he would be carrying
them in a trunk with a Hubbs’s lock. And I knew that my uncle had
a key to that lock.”

“So you stole the key?”

“No, I didn't steal it. I borrowed it. I knew where my uncle kept
it, and I took it one day when he was out of the office. Then I
had a duplicate made.”

“But Hubbs’s locks are unique!” I cried. “You couldn't have a
duplicate made!”

“Not an ordinary duplicate, no. But I know a man—a very clever
man—who can make a key to fit any lock. It took him a long time,
but he did it in the end.”

“And then?”

“Then I waited for my chance. I knew that Philip was sailing on
the _Olympia_, so I took a passage on the same boat. I watched
him all the time, and when I saw him leave his cabin for a few
minutes, I slipped in and opened the trunk.”

“But why did you try to force the lock?”

“To make it look like an outside job. I wanted people to think
that someone had tried to break in and then given up.”

“And then you took the bonds and sold them in New York?”

“Yes. I knew that the boat would be searched, so I didn't keep
them on me. I hid them in a safe place on board, and then, just
before we docked, I went and got them.”

“But how did you get them ashore?”

“I didn't. I gave them to a confederate who was waiting for me
on the pier.”

“And who was that confederate?”

“It was—it was Miss Farquhar!”

“Miss Farquhar!” I cried. “But she was the one who came to us!”

“Yes,” said Poirot. “She came to us to divert suspicion from
herself and her lover. She is a very clever woman, Hastings. A
very clever woman indeed.”

“But why did she call him Philip Ridgeway?”

“Because she wanted us to think that he was the victim, not the
criminal. She knew that if we thought he was Philip Ridgeway, we
would never suspect him of the theft.”

“And the grey hair?”

“A touch of theatrical powder, my friend. A very simple device,
but very effective.”

“And now,” said Poirot, turning to Vavasour, “I think you had
better come with us. There is an Inspector McNeil who would like
to have a word with you.”

Vavasour sighed and stood up.

“I suppose you're right,” he said. “The game is up.”

And so, with Poirot leading the way, we escorted Guy Vavasour
to the purser’s office, where he was handed over to the authorities.

“A very interesting case, Hastings,” said Poirot, as we walked
back to our cabin. “A very interesting case indeed.”

“But Poirot,” I said, “how did you know? How did you know it was
Guy Vavasour?”

“It was the hair, my friend,” said Poirot, smiling. “The hair at
the temples. It was too grey, too suddenly grey. And then there
was the fact that Miss Farquhar was so very anxious to help us.
She was a little too anxious, I thought. And when I saw Guy
Vavasour on the boat, I knew that I was right.”

“But how did you know he was Guy Vavasour?”

“I didn't. I only knew that he wasn't Philip Ridgeway. And then
I saw his name on the passenger list, and I put two and two
together.”

“You are a marvel, Poirot!” I cried. “A positive marvel!”

“No, no, my friend,” said Poirot modestly. “It is only the little
grey cells. The little grey cells!”

“I see,” said Poirot. “And this key of yours, Mr. Shaw—it remained in the Bank’s safe during your illness?”

“Exactly,” replied Mr. Shaw. “In the private safe to which only Mr. Vavasour and myself have the combination. It was never removed until my return to duty yesterday.”

“A most regrettable timing for an illness,” murmured Poirot. “It began, you say, on the very morning of the twenty-third?”

“A sudden and most violent attack of bronchitis,” explained Mr. Shaw with a slight, lingering cough. “I was strictly confined to my bed for more than a week.”

“Severe bronchitis is no joke to a man of my age,” said Mr. Shaw
ruefully. “But I am afraid Mr. Vavasour has suffered from the hard
work entailed by my absence, especially with this unexpected worry
coming on top of everything.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “And while you were indisposed, Monsieur Shaw, where was your key to the trunk?”

“In my private drawer here at the bank,” replied Shaw. “Locked, of course. I have the only key to that drawer on my person.”

“And yours, Monsieur Vavasour?”

“Always in my pocket,” the uncle replied, patting his waistcoat. “It has not left me for a moment. You see, Monsieur Poirot, we took every precaution. The bonds were sealed in the package using my own signet ring, and the package was placed in the trunk in our presence.”

“Well, I think that is all I have to ask you, gentlemen,” said
Poirot, rising. “I must make further inquiries at the docks.
Perhaps I can get some further light on this mysterious robbery.
At present the case is a very difficult one. Good-morning.”

“What an extraordinary thing!” said I, when we were once more in
the street. “Poirot, you really are a most amazing man! Why, you
haven’t asked them half the things you wanted to know! You
didn’t even ask them about the keys, for instance!”

“_Mon ami_,” said Poirot, with a grin. “Have I not told you that
the solution of every problem is a question of little grey cells?”

“Then why should we go to the docks?” I asked.

“We are not going to the docks. We are going to find a very clever
young lady.”

“Miss Farquhar?”

“The same.”

“What has she to do with it?”

“You will see, my friend. She may be able to tell us something that
Mr. Vavasour and Mr. Shaw have forgotten.”

“And during your illness, Mr. Shaw,” Poirot inquired, “your key remained here at the Bank?” “It was placed in the private safe,” Mr. Vavasour explained, “of which I alone hold the duplicate key. I can assure you, Monsieur Poirot, that it was never touched until my colleague returned to his duties. The security was absolute.” Poirot sighed, a sound of gentle melancholy. “Absolute security, and yet the million dollars, they fly away! It is a problem of the most fascinating, is it not, Hastings?”

“Is there any other person who could have had a key to the safe?”
asked Poirot.

“None,” said Mr. Vavasour. “Only my colleague and myself have the
combination.”

“I see. Now, Mr. Shaw, would you be so kind as to let me see your
key?”

Mr. Shaw produced it from his pocket-book.

“And yours, Mr. Vavasour?”

Mr. Vavasour produced his from his watch-chain.

“Thank you,” said Poirot. “I suppose that the bonds were already
in the portmanteau when you saw them?”

“No,” said Mr. Vavasour. “We counted them first and then put them
into the portmanteau and locked it.”

“And it was then, I suppose, that you found the lock was so very
much out of order?”

Mr. Vavasour looked at him in surprise.

“The lock? Oh, no, it was in perfect order.”

“You are sure of that?”

“Perfectly sure.”

Poirot’s eyes flickered.

“Thank you, gentlemen,” he said, rising. “I think that is all.”

“It was indeed a most unfortunate coincidence,” Poirot commented
sympathetically. “And these two keys—they have remained in the
safe of the Bank since the morning of the 23rd? You will pardon
the request, but might I be permitted to see them?” Mr. Vavasour
assented at once and, opening a small wall-safe, produced the
two keys. Poirot examined them with meticulous care for a moment
before returning them with a little bow of thanks. “Everything
is in order. And now, messieurs, I will not further take up
your time. I have much to reflect upon.”

Poirot asked a few more questions. I judged that he was endeavouring
to gauge the exact amount of intimacy between uncle and nephew.
Mr. Vavasour’s answers were brief and punctilious. His nephew was
a trusted official of the Bank, and had no debts or money
difficulties that he knew of. He had been entrusted with similar
missions in the past. Finally we were politely bowed out.

“I am disappointed,” said Poirot, as we emerged into the street.

“You hoped to discover more? They are such stodgy old men.”

“It is not their stodginess, Hastings. It is that I have not yet the—how shall I say?—the grand idea. Everything is so... as it should be. The robbery, it is a robbery of the most classic. And yet, there is a small thing—a very small thing—that does not please me. Why should the thief be so remarkably industrious as to scratch the lock and then, suddenly, find the key? It is an illogicality, and as you know, I do not like the lack of logic. It suggests a theatre, a mise-en-scène, and I ask myself: for whose benefit was this little drama of the scratched lock performed?”

“It is not their stodginess that disappoints me, Hastings. It is the lack of imagination! But come, let us consider the facts. The bonds are stolen. They are sold in New York before the ship even touches the quay. How is this possible? There is the wireless, but one does not ‘wireless’ a bond. There is the speed—the _Olympia_ is a fast ship, but even she cannot outrun the electricity. And then, there are those scratches on the lock. Why scratches, if one has the key?
