It is an aesthetic blunder, Hastings!”

“It is not that they are stodgy, Hastings. It is that they are so—how shall I say it?—transparent. And yet, there is a small detail that does not please me. Why, for instance, did the thief attempt to force the lock? If he had a key, he would use it. If he did not have a key, and could not force it, how did he eventually open it? It is a contradiction, you see. And then there is the matter of the time. The bonds were sold in New York within half an hour of the docking. That is very quick, my friend—marvellously quick!”

“It is not their stodginess that bothers me, Hastings. It is the lock! Why would a thief—a thief who possesses a key—take the trouble to scratch and mar the woodwork around the lock? It is a contradiction, an absurdity! And then, there is the matter of the time. The bonds were sold in New York almost before the *Olympia* arrived. Does that not strike you as remarkable?”

“It is not their stodginess that I mind,” said Poirot. “It is their lack of imagination. But tell me, Hastings, did you notice anything about the appearance of Mr. Shaw? He has been ill, he says, with severe bronchitis; yet his face is as brown as a berry, as though he had been seeking the sun rather than keeping his room. And then there is the matter of the lock. Why, my friend, should a man who has a key waste time in trying to force the lock? It is an absurdity! It is more than an absurdity—it is a clue!”

“It is not their stodginess which disappoints me, _mon ami_. I do
not expect to find in a Bank manager a ‘keen financier with an
eagle glance’ as your favourite works of fiction put it. No, I am
disappointed in the case—it is too easy!”

“Easy?”

“Yes, do you not find it almost childishly simple?”

“You know who stole the bonds?”

“I do.”

“But then—we must—why——”

“Do not confuse and fluster yourself, Hastings. We are not going
to do anything at present.”

“But why? What are you waiting for?”

“For the _Olympia_. She is due on her return trip from New York on
Tuesday.”

“But if you know who stole the bonds, why wait? He may escape.”

“He will not escape. He is too much the gentleman for that! And
even if he did, he can be caught. No, I have my reasons, and you
will see them on Tuesday evening. Meantime, let us go and eat some
of those little cakes at the place in Regent Street.”

“You are very mysterious, Poirot.”

“It is my nature. _Tiens!_ I will tell you one thing—this case was
decided the moment I saw the scratch on the lock of the trunk.”

“The scratch on the lock?”

“Yes, exactly. It was so very significant!”

“I suppose you will not tell me any more?”

“Not yet, Hastings. But you will have your thrill on Tuesday!”

“He cannot escape, my dear friend. He is far too respectable. He
would never dream of escaping. He will stay where he is and go on
with his work as usual.”

“Then it’s one of those two old men! Poirot, how can you be so
extraordinary? You think it’s Mr. Shaw or Mr. Vavasour?”

“I will not tell you which, Hastings, but I will tell you that it
is one of those four people we have seen to-day.”

“And Miss Farquhar?”

“I see no reason to exclude the charming Miss Farquhar from my
calculations, though I do not suspect her.”

“Then it’s one of the others? Philip Ridgeway, perhaps?”

“Ridgeway is most certainly a suspect. He was on the _Olympia_.
He had the bonds in his possession. He may have made away with
them.”

“But he came to you to find them!”

“A very common ruse, Hastings.”

“But the bonds were sold in New York while he was still on the
ship!”

“That is the point. That is where I shall begin my investigation.”

“Where? At New York?”

“No, on the _Olympia_ when she docks at Liverpool on Tuesday.”

“But she’s been searched already!”

“I am not going to search her for the bonds, Hastings. I am going
to look for something else.”

“What?”

“A very small thing, my friend. A very small thing indeed.”

Tuesday morning found us at Liverpool. We were met by Inspector
McNeil, a quiet, capable-looking man. He greeted Poirot with a
certain amount of respect, though I could see that he was a little
puzzled as to the reason for our visit.

“The ship will be in in about an hour, Mr. Poirot,” he said. “But
I’m afraid you won’t find anything more than we have. We’ve been
over every inch of her.”

“I am sure of it, Inspector,” said Poirot. “I do not expect to
find anything you have overlooked. I am merely following a little
theory of my own.”

“Well, you’re welcome to try, of course. I’ll come with you if you
like.”

“I should be charmed. And I want to see the cabin occupied by Mr.
Ridgeway.”

“Certainly. It’s No. 34 on the ‘C’ deck.”

“No, my friend, I assure you that he cannot escape. Besides, I
want to be certain of one or two minor details.”

Tuesday came at last, and with it the arrival of the _Olympia_.
Poirot and I were on the quay, and we saw the first of the passengers
disembark. It was quite early in the afternoon.

“Well,” said Poirot, “I think we will go and see Mr. Ridgeway.”

We found him in his room at the Bank. He looked if possible more
haggard than when we had last seen him.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot? Any news?”

“I have much news for you, Mr. Ridgeway. But first I would like
to see your uncle.”

He led the way into the managers’ room. Both Mr. Vavasour and Mr.
Shaw were there. They looked at Poirot with a certain amount of
coldness.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot?” they both said together. “Have you
discovered anything?”

“My dear friend, he cannot escape. He is already caught.”

“But who is he?”

“I shall tell you—on Wednesday morning.”

I sighed. Poirot’s mysteries were often like this, and I had
learned to wait. On Tuesday morning we were at Liverpool when the
_Olympia_ berthed, and I confess I was somewhat surprised at
Poirot’s methods. He went on board and requested an interview with
one of the stewards.

“I want to ask you a question,” he said. “Do you remember the day
before the _Olympia_ sailed? A young man, dark, with a slight
moustache, came on board?”

The steward looked puzzled.

“So many young men do that, sir,” he said. “He might have been one
of the passengers.”

“This one was not a passenger. He came on board just for a few
minutes, perhaps to see a friend. He was in a hurry.”

The steward shook his head.

“I can’t say I remember him particularly, sir.”

“Because I want to make sure of something, Hastings. A little
detail which is lacking at present. I should be glad to know for
certain how the bonds were stolen.”

“But you said you knew!”

“I know _who_ stole them. I do not yet know _how_ they were stolen.”

“I must say you are very mysterious, Poirot.”

“It is my nature to be mysterious, as you know. Tuesday should
give us our answer. In the meantime, I shall take a little holiday
and spend it at the seaside.”

“Where?”

“At Liverpool.”

“But that isn’t a seaside resort!”

“To me it is. It has the sea and it has ships. What more do you
want?”

Tuesday morning found us at the Liverpool docks, awaiting the
arrival of the _Olympia_. Poirot had already obtained a pass
from the Steamship Company, and we went on board as soon as she
was alongside.

A steward was told off to attend to us.

“I want to see the cabin Mr. Philip Ridgeway occupied on his trip
to New York.”

“Yes, sir. This way, sir. Cabin C.54.”

The cabin was a large and comfortable one on the promenade deck.
Poirot went over it with a magnifying-glass, but without result.

“You see nothing, Hastings?”

“Nothing.”

“And I see nothing. That is as it should be.”

He turned to the steward.

“Can you tell me who occupied this cabin on the trip from New
York?”

“A Mr. and Mrs. Henderson, sir.”

“They were elderly people?”

“Yes, sir. About sixty or so, I should judge.”

“They went ashore early?”

“Yes, sir. As soon as we docked.”

“And their luggage—did they have much?”

“Only two small suitcases and a Gladstone bag, sir.”

“Thank you.”

Poirot drew me out on to the deck.

“You have it now, Hastings? The solution of the mystery?”

“I have not the slightest idea!”

“But it is so simple! The person who stole the bonds was——”

“Who?”

“Wait! We must have a little scene—a little drama. Let us go back
to London.”

“To a South Sea island where there is no extradition? No, _mon
ami_, he would find life very uncongenial there. As to why I
wait—_eh bien_ to the intelligence of Hercule Poirot the case is
perfectly clear, but for the benefit of others, not so greatly
gifted by the good God—the Inspector McNeil, for instance—it would
be as well to make a few inquiries to establish the facts. One must
have consideration for those less gifted than oneself.”

“Good Lord, Poirot! Do you know, I’d give a considerable sum of
money to see you make a thorough ass of yourself—just for once.
You’re so confoundedly conceited!”

“Do not enrage yourself, Hastings. In verity, I observe that there
are times when you almost detest me! Alas, I suffer the penalties
of greatness!”

The little man puffed out his chest, and sighed so comically that
I was forced to laugh.

The next few days were passed in some suspense, as Poirot was very
secretive about his movements. On Tuesday afternoon, however, he
requested me to accompany him to the headquarters of the London
and Scottish Bank. We were received by Mr. Vavasour, and to our
surprise Mr. Shaw was also in the room.

“I have much pleasure in informing you, gentlemen,” said Poirot,
“that the case of the Liberty Bonds is now at an end.”

The two men stared at him.

“You mean you have found the thief?” cried Mr. Vavasour.

“I have,” said Poirot, “and I have the proof also. But first, let
us go back to the beginning. The bonds were in a locked trunk.
The trunk had a special lock. But, as Mr. Ridgeway so justly remarked,
if the thief had the key, why should he waste time trying to force
the lock?”

“Exactly,” said Mr. Vavasour. “Why?”

“Because he had _not_ got the key,” said Poirot. “He only had the
impression of it!”

“But how could he get an impression of a key that was never out
of Mr. Ridgeway’s possession?”

“Ah, but it was out of his possession once! When he was being
searched at New York!”

“But the bonds were stolen before he reached New York!”

“Pardon, they were not. They were stolen on the morning of the
23rd, _before the Olympia left Liverpool_.”

“But that is impossible! They were counted and sealed in Mr.
Ridgeway’s presence only a few hours before!”

“Exactly. And the seal was an imitation. It was all a very clever
plot. The bonds were never in the trunk at all!”

“But—but—then where were they?”

“They were in the possession of the man who stole them—Mr. Shaw!”

The following Tuesday morning, I was at the docks when the _Olympia_
was signaled. Poirot was there, too, and we soon found our way
aboard her and into the purser’s office.

“I am Hercule Poirot,” announced my friend. “I have been asked
by the London and Scottish Bank to investigate the theft of the
Liberty Bonds on your last voyage.”

“We were nearly crazy over it, I can tell you,” said the purser.
“Not a thing we didn’t do to find them. The Captain was nearly
fit to be tied!”

“Exactly, exactly! You will allow me to ask you a few questions?”

“Why, certainly! I’ll tell you all I can.”

“The steward of Mr. Ridgeway’s cabin, where is he?”

“Oh, that’s easy! He’s in the sick-bay. Broke his leg just as we
were leaving New York.”

“I see. And the steward who took his place?”

“Oh, he’s about somewhere—no, wait a minute, he isn’t! He was
only signed on for the one trip. He left us at New York.”

Poirot’s eyes flashed with a sudden light.

“Ah! He left you at New York, did he? What was his name?”

“Let me see—Pridhu—Pridhu—no, that’s not it. Ah, I have it—Pridhu—no,
it was Pringle—James Pringle.”

“Aha!” said Poirot, and his eyes fairly danced with delight. “And
he was a small man, was he not? With a slight limp?”

“Why, yes, he was! How did you know?”

“I have a little—how do you say?—instinct for these things,” said
Poirot, with a wave of his hand. “Now, one more thing. I should
like to see the cabin occupied by Mr. Ridgeway.”

The purser led the way, and Poirot spent some minutes in a
minute inspection of the cabin and the trunk which stood under the
bunk.

“It has been repaired, I see,” he remarked, as he rose from his
knees. “The lock, I mean. Well, I have seen all I want to see.
Many thanks to you, Monsieur.”

He walked away, whistling a little tune to himself.

“Well, Poirot?” I asked, as we paced the deck together. “Have you
found out anything?”

“Everything, my friend!”

“Then who was it?”

“Wait a little, wait a little! I must first go to the Bank and
see Mr. Vavasour and Mr. Shaw.”

“But you know who it was?”

“I know who it was, yes.”

“Then why not tell me? It’s most annoying of you!”

“Because it is much more artistic to wait and tell everyone
at once. Come, we will go to the Bank.”

Mr. Vavasour and Mr. Shaw were in their room as before. Poirot
greeted them with a polite bow.

“I have come to report the result of my investigations,” he said.
“I have been to the _Olympia_, and I have seen the cabin where the
theft took place.”

“And you have found—what?” asked Mr. Vavasour.

“I have found the thief,” said Poirot.

The two men stared at him in amazement.

“The thief? You know who it was?”

“I know who it was, yes.”

“Then—who was it?”

“It was Mr. Shaw,” said Poirot.

Mr. Shaw started back with a cry of indignation.

“What! You dare to accuse me?”

“I do,” said Poirot. “And I will tell you how you did it. You
knew that the bonds were to be sent over to New York, and you knew
that Mr. Ridgeway was to take them. You also knew that you would
be able to get the key of the trunk, because you ordered the lock
yourself. You then engaged a man to act as steward on the
_Olympia_, and you gave him the key. He was to steal the bonds and
bring them to you in New York. You yourself went to New York on
another ship, and you met him there. You then sold the bonds, and
returned to England as soon as you could.”

“It’s a lie!” cried Mr. Shaw. “A wicked lie!”

“Is it?” said Poirot. “Then perhaps you can explain how it was
that the steward, James Pringle, was so like you in appearance?
And how it was that he had a slight limp, just as you have?”

Mr. Shaw turned pale and sank into a chair.

“It’s no use,” he said. “I see you know everything. Yes, I did
it. I was in difficulties, and I saw a chance of getting the money.
I thought I could manage it so that no one would ever know.”

“And the bonds?” asked Mr. Vavasour.

“I have some of them still,” said Mr. Shaw. “The rest—well, the
rest are gone.”

“But how did you manage it?” I asked. “How did you get the bonds
on board the _Olympia_ without being seen?”

“I didn’t,” said Poirot. “The bonds were never on board the
_Olympia_ at all. They were stolen before they ever left the Bank.”

“But Mr. Ridgeway saw them put into the trunk!” I cried.

“He saw a package put into the trunk,” said Poirot. “But it was
not the package containing the bonds. That had been changed for
another one. Mr. Shaw had managed to get hold of the bonds and
put them into another package, which he then took to New York himself.
He then gave the steward the key of the trunk, and told him to
make it look as if it had been broken into, so as to divert
suspicion. The steward then left the ship at New York, and met
Mr. Shaw there. It was all very simple, once you had the key.”

“But the steward?” I asked. “What became of him?”

“Oh, he is still in New York, I expect,” said Poirot. “He was only
a tool in the hands of Mr. Shaw. Well, Mr. Vavasour, I think you
will find that most of the bonds can be recovered. And now, if
you will excuse me, I think I will go and tell Miss Farquhar and
Mr. Ridgeway the good news.”

And with a polite bow, Poirot led the way out of the room.

“Well, Poirot,” I said, as we walked down the street. “You certainly
did it that time. But how did you know it was Mr. Shaw?”

“It was the lock, my friend,” said Poirot. “The lock that they
tried to force, and then opened with a key. That told me at once
that someone who had the key must be the thief. And as only three
people had the key, it was not difficult to find out which one
it was. Mr. Vavasour had no reason to steal the bonds, and Mr.
Ridgeway would hardly have stolen them and then told everyone
about it. That left only Mr. Shaw. And when I found out about the
steward, I was sure of it.”

“Well,” I said, “you certainly are a wonder, Poirot!”

“Am I not?” said Poirot, with a smile. “But then, as I have often
told you, I am Hercule Poirot!”

During the following days, Poirot was busy in his own way. He
disappeared for hours together, and when he returned he would give
no account of his doings. He only smiled and looked more satisfied
than ever.

On Monday evening he said to me: “Tomorrow morning, Hastings, we
must see the _Olympia_ as she comes into dock. We will be there
betimes.”

It was early indeed when we reached the riverside. Poirot led the
way on board, and sought out the purser. From him he obtained some
details of the voyage, and we then were shown down to the cabins
of the first class.

The purser showed us a large, comfortable cabin.

“This was the one Mr. Ridgeway had,” he said.

Poirot spent some time in examining the door and the lock. Then he
turned to the purser.

“Now, about those keys. I think you told me that the keys were
kept in a small safe in the Purser’s office?”

“Yes, Monsieur Poirot.”

“And who had access to it?”

“Only myself and my assistant.”

“You are sure of that?”

“Quite sure.”

“The safe was always locked?”

“Always.”

“Well, let us go and see.”

The purser led the way to his office. On the wall was a small safe.
Poirot examined it, and then the keys which the purser produced.

“A very simple lock,” he observed. “A skeleton key could open it in
two minutes. But tell me, who was this assistant of yours?”

“A very steady young fellow, of the name of Shaw.”

“Shaw? That is a common name. What was he like?”

“A tall, thin young man with a slight limp.”

“Aha! Now I think we have found what we were looking for. I am
obliged to you, Monsieur.”

We left the ship and Poirot hurried me away in a taxi.

“What was that about Shaw?” I asked.

“Wait and see, Hastings, wait and see!” was all the satisfaction I
got.

We drove to the London and Scottish Bank, and were once more shown
up into the room where the two managers were sitting. They looked
at us with some surprise.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot? Any news?” asked Mr. Vavasour.

“I think I may say I have found the thief,” said Poirot calmly.

The two men started.

“Who was it?” they cried together.

Poirot turned to Mr. Shaw.

“I think you can tell us that, Monsieur,” he said, with a smile.

The man turned a ghastly white.

“I—I——” he stammered.

“You see, Monsieur Shaw, your nephew—or should I say your son?—was
very useful to you in this little matter. He was the assistant
purser on the _Olympia_, and he took care that the bonds should
never reach America at all.”

“What do you mean?” cried Mr. Vavasour.

“I mean that the bonds were never in the portmanteau at all! They
were stolen before they ever left the Bank!”

“But we saw them put in ourselves!”

“You saw a package of bonds put in, but they were not the Liberty
Bonds. They were a lot of worthless paper which had been
substituted for them. The real bonds were sold in London, not New
York, before the _Olympia_ ever sailed!”

“But the numbers?”

“The numbers were cabled to New York by the thief himself, who
took care to see that they were the numbers of the bonds he had
already sold in London. It was a very clever scheme, but it had
one flaw—the thief forgot that the numbers of the bonds sold in
New York would not agree with those sold in London!”

“And who is the thief?” asked Mr. Vavasour.

Poirot pointed a finger at Mr. Shaw.

“There is your man!” he said. “He was the only person who had the
opportunity and the knowledge necessary to carry out such a
daring robbery. He substituted the bonds in the Bank, and his son,
the assistant purser, did the rest.”

Mr. Shaw made a sudden movement towards the door, but Poirot was
too quick for him.

“No, no, my friend! The police are waiting outside. It is no use.”

With a groan, the wretched man sank back into his chair.

“It is true,” he said hoily. “I was in difficulties—I thought I could
replace the money before it was discovered—but it was no use.”

“And so,” said Poirot, as we walked away from the Bank, “the mystery
is solved. A very simple case, Hastings, as I told you.”

“But how did you find out about the son?” I asked.

“Ah, that was a little piece of luck. I happened to see a photograph
of him in Mr. Shaw’s house, and I recognized him at once as the
man I had seen on the _Olympia_.”

“But you never went to Mr. Shaw’s house!”

“Ah, but I did, Hastings! While you were asleep in your bed, I
was busy making inquiries. And now, let us go and have some lunch.
I think we have earned it.”

And as we sat in our favourite restaurant, Poirot leaned back in
his chair with a sigh of satisfaction.

“A very pretty case,” he murmured. “A very pretty case indeed!”

“But Poirot,” I said, “you haven’t told me one thing. Why did the
thief try to force the lock of the portmanteau if he had the key
all the time?”

Poirot smiled.

“To draw attention to the fact that the bonds had been stolen from
the portmanteau, of course! If the lock had not been tampered with,
it might have been days before the loss was discovered, and by that
time the thief would have had plenty of time to escape. No, it was
a very clever touch, that!”

“I see,” I said. “Well, Poirot, I must take off my hat to you. You’ve
certainly done it this time!”

“I always do, Hastings, I always do!” said the little man, with a
twinkle in his eye.

And as I looked at him, I could not help thinking that, for all his
conceit, there was no one quite like Hercule Poirot.

THE END

“One small point I have to look up,” he said. “A most important
small point. And after that—wait until the _Olympia_ returns.”

The days passed, and I noticed that Poirot was constantly in the
city. He would be away for hours together, and would return
looking more than ever like a cat that had eaten the cream.

On the Wednesday, as we were sitting at tea in our rooms, he
remarked casually:

“I saw Miss Farquhar this morning.”

“What did she say?”

“She is still very anxious. Her Philip is still under a cloud.
He is being watched by Scotland Yard, and at any moment may be
arrested. She is a brave girl, that Miss Esmée. She does not
doubt him for an instant.”

“Well, I’m glad some one is pleased with you, Poirot. I can’t say
I see that you’ve done much to help the poor young fellow.”

“No? You will see. I have asked them all to come here this evening.”

“The Bank managers?”

“Yes, and the young man and his fiancée. Also, Inspector McNeil.
That will be quite a party, will it not?”

I felt some excitement at his words. Was he really going to
unmask the thief, or was it a mere piece of bluff?

At eight o’clock they arrived, the two Bank managers, looking
grave and important, Philip Ridgeway, pale and anxious, and Miss
Farquhar, whose face was flushed with excitement. Inspector
McNeil brought up the rear. He looked at Poirot with some amusement
and a good deal of curiosity.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot,” he said, as he took a chair. “You have
found out who stole the bonds, I hear.”

“I have,” said Poirot, with a little bow. “And I will proceed at
once to tell you what happened. It is quite simple. The bonds
never went on the _Olympia_ at all!”

“What?” cried Ridgeway. “Why, I saw them put in the trunk!”

“You saw a package, Mr. Ridgeway, which you were told contained the
bonds. You did not see them actually put in.”

“But I saw them counted!”

“Were they counted in your presence?”

“Well—no—not exactly. My uncle and Mr. Shaw had already counted
them when I arrived.”

“Exactly. You were shown a package, sealed with the Bank’s seal,
and you were told it contained the bonds. You placed it in your
trunk, and you locked the trunk. But, my friend, that package did
_not_ contain the bonds. It contained—paper!”

A gasp of astonishment went round the room.

“But—the theft—the scratched lock!” cried Philip.

“The scratched lock was a very clever piece of work. It was
intended to make it appear that an attempt had been made to force
the lock—an attempt which had failed. But the thief had the key!”

“But how could he? I have the only one!”

“Except for the two others which were in the Bank’s safe. One
belonged to Mr. Vavasour, the other to Mr. Shaw.”

All eyes were turned on the two Bank managers. Mr. Vavasour was
the first to speak.

“This is a very serious charge, Monsieur Poirot. Do you realise
what you are saying?”

“Perfectly. I am saying that one of you two gentlemen is the
thief.”

Mr. Shaw half rose from his chair.

“This is monstrous!” he cried. “I have been ill—I have not been
near the Bank for a fortnight!”

“Precisely,” said Poirot. “And that gave you the opportunity you
needed. You were not ill at all. You were in New York!”

“In New York?”

“Yes. You left for New York on the _Gigantic_, which sailed two
days before the _Olympia_. You arrived in New York several hours
before the _Olympia_ docked. You had the bonds with you. You sold
them, and then you returned to England by the next boat. I have
verified your movements, Mr. Shaw. I have also found the doctor
who attended you—or rather, the doctor who _didn't_ attend you, for
he was a myth!”

For a moment there was a dead silence. Then Mr. Shaw made a sudden
dash for the door. But Inspector McNeil was too quick for him.

“No, you don't!” he said, as he gripped him by the arm. “I think
you’d better come with me, Mr. Shaw.”

As the door closed behind them, Miss Farquhar ran to Philip and
put her arms round his neck.

“Oh, Philip, I knew it! I knew it!”

Mr. Vavasour was looking at Poirot in a dazed way.

“I can hardly believe it,” he murmured. “Shaw! A man I have
trusted for years!”

“It is often the way,” said Poirot sententiously. “The most
trusted are the most tempted. And now, if you will excuse us, I
think we have all had enough excitement for one evening.”

When they had all gone, I turned to Poirot.

“Well, you’ve done it again, Poirot! But how on earth did you
guess?”

“It was the scratched lock, Hastings. That was the clue that
started me off. Why scratch the lock if you have the key? To make
people think you _haven't_ got it, of course. And who had the keys?
The two Bank managers and Ridgeway. Ridgeway was on the boat, so
it couldn't have been him. That left the two Bank managers. And
when I heard that Mr. Shaw had been ill—well, it was too good to be
true! I just had to verify it, that was all.”

“And the doctor?”

“There wasn't any doctor, as I suspected. Shaw just stayed at
home and let it be known he was ill. Then he slipped off to
Liverpool and caught the _Gigantic_. It was all very simple.”

“Well, Poirot,” I said, “I must take back what I said about your
being conceited. You’re a genius, and that’s all there is to it!”

“_Mon ami_,” said Poirot, “you are too kind. But, after all, it is
only the exercise of the little grey cells!”

“Come, come, Hastings, tell me what you would do in my place? To
whom would your suspicions point? To Mr. Ridgeway? He had the
opportunity, and his trunk was forced from the inside—at least the
lock was. Or to the uncle? He had the second key, and he knew
perfectly well what his nephew had in his possession. Or to the
third man, the joint general manager, who was ill on the day of
the sailing? He also had a key, but he was ill in bed!”

“And he is a most respectable man,” I put in. “Besides, it couldn’t
well be he, could it?”

“You are right, Hastings. One must not let oneself be led away by
prejudice. Let us concentrate on the facts. What do we know? That
the bonds were stolen and that they were sold in New York. Let us
start from that.”

“The sale of the bonds!” I cried. “But that was only half an hour
after the arrival of the _Olympia_. Even if the thief had jumped
overboard and swam for it, he couldn’t have reached the shore in
time!”

Tuesday saw us speeding to Liverpool in a first-class carriage of
the L. & N.W.R. Poirot had obstinately refused to enlighten me as
to his suspicions—or certainties. He contented himself with
expressing surprise that I, too, was not equally _au fait_ with
the situation. I disdained to argue, and entrenched my curiosity
behind a rampart of pretended indifference.

On arrival at Liverpool we were met by Inspector McNeil. He was a
tall, soldierly-looking man, and greeted Poirot with great respect.

“The boat is just in, Mr. Poirot,” he said. “If you like to come
along to the docks, I have a car waiting.”

We were soon speeding through the streets of Liverpool.

“I am wondering if you will allow me to take the lead in this
matter?” said Poirot. “I have a little idea, you see.”

The Inspector grinned. “I know those little ideas of yours, Mr.
Poirot. Go right ahead.”

“First of all, then, I should like to interview the steward who
looked after Mr. Ridgeway.”

The Inspector made the necessary arrangements, and we were soon
seated in the steward’s own little room. He was a man with a
somewhat shiftful eye and a nervous manner.

“Now, my man,” said Poirot. “I want you to tell me exactly what
happened on the morning that Mr. Ridgeway’s trunk was found tampered
with?”

We reached our destination in the afternoon and went straight to
the docks. The _Olympia_ had already docked. Poirot led the way
straight to the purser’s office.

“I have a letter of introduction here from Mr. Vavasour of the
London and Scottish Bank,” said Poirot. “He gave it to me for you
on the chance of your having some additional information to give
me on this business of the stolen bonds.”

The purser looked at it.

“You’re Monsieur Poirot? Yes, I heard something about your being
called in. But I’m afraid I can’t tell you more than I told the
police. It’s a complete mystery to me how it was done.”

“Quite so,” said Poirot. “I suppose you have many people coming
on board at the last moment?”

“A few—friends of the passengers mostly. They have to leave before
the ship sails, of course.”

“Yes, I know. Now, did any of the passengers join the ship late?”

“Only one—Mr. Shaw, of the London and Scottish Bank.”

“Mr. Shaw?” I cried. “But he was in bed with bronchitis.”

“It’s the first I’ve heard of it then,” said the purser. “He was
here all right, for I spoke to him myself.”

“Ah!” said Poirot. “This is most interesting. Can you describe
him?”

“Well, he’s a middle-aged man, with a grey beard.”

“A grey beard?” I said. “But Mr. Shaw is clean shaven.”

Poirot nudged me to be silent.

“And he stayed on board?”

“No, he only came to see Mr. Ridgeway for a few minutes before we
sailed. He left just before the gangway was hauled up.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “And did any one else come to see Mr.
Ridgeway?”

“No one that I know of.”

“And Mr. Ridgeway’s cabin was No. 37, wasn’t it?”

“Yes.”

“Thank you very much. That is all I wanted to know.”

He turned away and I followed him.

We arrived at Liverpool in time to meet the _Olympia_ as she came
alongside the quay. Poirot inquired for the purser and we were
shown at once to his office. He was a small, alert-looking man,
and he listened with some attention to Poirot’s credentials.

“Anything you wish to see, Mr. Poirot? Oh, that bond case! Yes,
I remember it well—I had a good deal to do with it myself.”

“Could I see the cabin Mr. Ridgeway occupied?”

“Certainly. It is empty this trip.”

The purser led the way and we followed him along several
corridors. He unlocked the door of a small outside cabin. Poirot
went in, and stood for a moment in the centre of it.

“And the trunk was—where?”

“Under the bunk. There!”

Poirot got down on his knees and began to examine the wood-work of
the bunk.

“The lock was scratched, you say? Ah, yes, I see. A clumsy piece
of work.”

He stood up and began to finger the handle of the door.

“And this door, was it kept locked?”

“Only when the passenger was out of his cabin.”

“I see. Now, Monsieur the Purser, I should like to ask you one
question. Did you see the bonds yourself?”

“No, I didn’t see them, but I saw the package.”

“And it was—what size?”

“Oh, quite a small package, about seven inches by four, I should
say.”

Poirot’s eyes opened.

“So small as that?”

“Yes, it wasn’t at all a large package.”

“Thank you, Monsieur. That is all I wanted to know.”

We went back to the purser’s office. Poirot appeared to be
thinking deeply.

“One more thing,” he said, as we reached the door. “Did you have
many passengers this trip?”

“No, very few. It’s the slack season.”

“Any one of the name of—er—Vavasour?”

“No.”

“Or Shaw?”

“No.”

“Or—Ridgeway?”

“No.”

“Thank you. Good-morning.”

He walked away with a smile on his face.

“Well?” I asked.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of it?”

“I don’t know what to think. Those bonds must have been stolen by
one of those four people we were talking about. And yet—if they
weren’t on the ship——”

“Who said they weren’t on the ship?”

“But they were sold in New York within half an hour of her
docking!”

“Exactly. And how could they be sold in New York if they were in
a trunk on the _Olympia_? Answer me that, Hastings!”

“They couldn’t, of course.”

“Therefore they weren’t in the trunk. That is what I have been
trying to tell you all along.”

“Then Philip Ridgeway——”

“Wait, wait! Do not jump to conclusions. We must go back to London
and see—someone.”

“Who?”

“Mr. Shaw.”

At Liverpool we had a short interview with the Captain and his
officers on the _Olympia_. Poirot’s questions were brief and to
the point. He seemed satisfied. From the _Olympia_ we went to the
local branch of the London and Scottish Bank, where again we spent
some time.

“Well, Poirot,” I said, as we emerged from its portals, “you have
found out what you wanted?”

“I have.”

“Then we go back to London?”

“No, we have an appointment with someone at his house here.
Wait, let me consult the address.”

“Whose house?”

“That of Mr. Shaw.”

“Mr. Shaw? But I thought he was in London?”

“He came down here yesterday on business. He was kind enough to
invite us to call.”

“Poirot, what on earth is the meaning of all this? Do you mean
to say that Mr. Shaw——”

“My dear Hastings, do not excite yourself. Here is the house.”

On arrival, Poirot led the way down the gangway and on to the
_Olympia_. The great liner was being berthed at the landing-stage,
and for once her decks were not thronged with excited passengers.
She was taking in coal.

A few words to a steward, and we were conducted to the cabin
Philip Ridgeway had occupied on the outward voyage. Poirot spent
ten minutes there, then he emerged and sought the purser’s office.
He requested to see the steward who had waited on Mr. Ridgeway.
The man, a stolid-looking individual, was soon found.

“Now, my friend,” said Poirot. “You remember Mr. Ridgeway who
crossed to New York a fortnight ago?”

“Yes, sir, I remember him perfectly.”

“Good. Now, on the morning of the day before you reached New York,
you were in his cabin, were you not?”

“Yes, sir, I was.”

“And you saw him?”

“Yes, sir. He was sitting at his table, writing.”

“And what was he doing?”

“Well, sir, he seemed to be busy over some papers, and his trunk
was open on the floor.”

“His trunk was open?”

“Yes, sir.”

“You are sure of that?”

“Quite sure, sir.”

“And did he seem to be in any way disturbed or—er—agitated?”

“Not that I noticed, sir.”

“That will do, thank you.”

Poirot turned to me with a look of triumph.

“You see, Hastings? He was sitting at his table, writing—with his
trunk open! Does that not suggest anything to you?”

“It suggests that he was a very careless young man,” I said
stiffly. “But I don’t see that it proves anything.”

“Wait and see, my friend. Wait and see!”

We next interviewed the ship’s doctor. He, too, remembered
Mr. Ridgeway.

“I was called to see him on the second day out,” he said. “He was
suffering from a very severe attack of sea-sickness.”

“Sea-sickness?” cried Poirot. “But surely—the _Olympia_—a boat of
that size—and in such weather as you had then!”

“It was a bit rough, certainly, but nothing to speak of. Still,
some people are very susceptible.”

“And how long did the attack last?”

“Oh, he was all right again by the next morning.”

“Thank you, doctor. That is all I wanted to know.”

As we walked away, Poirot’s eyes were sparkling with suppressed
excitement.

“Now, Hastings, for the final scene! We must get back to London
at once.”

“But what have you discovered?” I asked, in bewilderment.

“Everything, my friend! The whole plot is as clear as daylight.
But we must hurry—we must hurry!”

Once arrived at the quay alongside which lay the big transatlantic
liner, Poirot became brisk and alert. Our proceedings consisted in
interviewing four successive stewards and inquiring after a friend
of Poirot’s who had crossed to New York on the 23rd.

“An elderly gentleman, wearing glasses. A great invalid, hardly
moved out of his cabin.”

After some delay we were directed to the cabin steward of No. 12
on the main deck.

“Yes, sir,” said the man. “I remember him well. He was in bed
most of the voyage. Only came on deck once or twice. I think his
name was Mr. Shaw.”

Poirot’s eyes flashed for a second.

“Is that so? Well, I must have missed him after all. I should have
thought he would have been more on deck, but I expect his health
is still far from good.”

“He didn’t seem very grand, sir, certainly. A bit weak on his legs
and shaky in his hands.”

“Just so. Thank you very much.”

Poirot drew me away.

“Well, Hastings? You see?”

“I see—but I don’t understand! Mr. Shaw? But he was in London!”

“Was he? He was away from the Bank for a fortnight—with
bronchitis. A very convenient malady, bronchitis! It keeps you in
your room. You see no one.”

“But the bonds were stolen on the _Olympia_!”

“Exactly. By Mr. Shaw.”

“But how? He wasn’t on the _Olympia_!”

“My dear Hastings! He _was_ on the _Olympia_! He was the ‘invalid
gentleman’ in cabin No. 12!”

“But Ridgeway would have known him!”

“Ridgeway never saw him. The ‘invalid gentleman’ never left his
cabin. The steward saw him, but the steward did not know Mr. Shaw
of the London and Scottish Bank.”

“Then it was Shaw who stole the bonds?”

“It was Shaw who had the bonds all the time. He and Vavasour
planned it together. They are both in it. Vavasour was to stay in
London and keep up appearances, while Shaw, suitably disguised,
took the bonds across. They had the keys, remember.”

“But the search? And the bonds being sold in New York before the
_Olympia_ arrived?”

“Ah, that was the cleverest part of the whole thing! The bonds
were never on the _Olympia_ at all!”

“But I saw them put into the trunk!”

“You did nothing of the sort, Hastings! You saw a package, which
you were _told_ contained the bonds, put into the trunk. It
contained—nothing! Or rather, some old newspapers.”

“Then how were they sold in New York?”

“By the confederate who had gone over on a faster boat! The
_Mauretania_ sailed from Southampton on the same day as the
_Olympia_ from Liverpool, and she is a much faster boat. She would
reach New York a full day before the _Olympia_. The confederate—who
was probably one of the smaller fry of the Bank—had the bonds with
him. He sold them as soon as he landed. When the _Olympia_ arrived,
the theft was ‘discovered,’ and the numbers of the bonds
telegraphed out—but it was too late!”

“It’s incredible!” I exclaimed. “And yet—it’s so simple!”

“All great crimes are simple, Hastings! That is why they are so
often successful. But I think we have enough evidence now to
interest Inspector McNeil.”

“And Philip Ridgeway?”

“His character will be cleared, and he will no doubt marry the
charming Miss Farquhar and live happily ever afterwards. A
charming young lady, Hastings! I admire her immensely. She has
what you call the ‘grit’!”

We were back in London that evening. Poirot’s first care was to
communicate with Scotland Yard. The result was an interview the
following morning between Poirot, myself, and Inspector McNeil.

The Inspector was at first inclined to be skeptical.

“It’s a tall story, Monsieur Poirot,” he said. “But I’ll admit it
hangs together. If we can prove that Shaw was on the _Olympia_—well,
that’s about all we want.”

“The steward of cabin No. 12 will identify him,” said Poirot.

“We’ll see about that. I’ll go down to the Bank at once.”

We accompanied him. On arrival, we were told that Mr. Vavasour was
in his office, but that Mr. Shaw had not yet arrived.

“We will see Mr. Vavasour,” said the Inspector.

We were shown into the manager’s room. He looked up with a frown
as we entered.

“I am very busy this morning, gentlemen,” he said. “Is this matter
urgent?”

“Very urgent, Mr. Vavasour,” said the Inspector. “It’s about those
Liberty Bonds.”

Vavasour’s face changed. He looked from one to the other of us.

“What about them?” he asked.

“We have reason to believe,” said the Inspector, “that they were
never on the _Olympia_ at all.”

Vavasour’s face went a greyish white.

“I—I don’t understand,” he stammered.

“I think you do,” said the Inspector. “I have a warrant here for
your arrest, and also for that of Mr. Shaw.”

Vavasour sank back in his chair.

“It’s no use,” he muttered. “Shaw’s gone. He’s been gone since last
night. I suppose he’s got away.”

“Not he!” said the Inspector. “We’ll have him before the day’s out.
Now, Mr. Vavasour, I must ask you to come with me.”

As we left the Bank, Poirot turned to me with a smile.

“You see, Hastings? The ‘stodgy old men’! They were not so stodgy
after all!”

“But Shaw’s got away!”

“He will be caught, never fear. And even if he is not—well, we have
saved the reputation of a young man, and that is something.”

“And Miss Farquhar?”

“I think,” said Poirot, “that we will go and tell her the good
news ourselves.”

We found Miss Farquhar at her flat. She was overjoyed at the news.

“I knew Philip was innocent!” she cried. “I never doubted him for
a minute!”

“And now,” said Poirot, “he will be able to marry you and live
happily ever afterwards.”

“Thanks to you, Monsieur Poirot!”

“No, no,” said Poirot. “Thanks to the ‘little grey cells’! They
are very useful things, Hastings, very useful indeed!”

I think I have never seen Poirot more pleased with himself than
he was over this case. And I must admit that he had every reason
to be. For, as he said, it was a very neat little problem—and he
had solved it with his usual brilliance.

“There were several such, Monsieur,” said one of the stewards,
scratching his head. “I seem to remember one—an American, he was.
Suffering from lumbago, I think he said. Mr. Shaw, he called
himself.”

“Aha!” Poirot gave a start. “Mr. Shaw—you are sure of the name?”

“Yes, Monsieur, he was on my list, cabin 48.”

“Wait a bit,” I broke in. “Mr. Shaw is the joint general manager
of the Bank. He was ill with bronchitis on the 23rd.”

Poirot ignored my interruption and continued his questions.

“Was he a tall man, this Mr. Shaw?”

“Medium height, Monsieur, and heavily built.”

“Grey beard?”

“No, clean shaven, Monsieur.”

“I see. And he had a companion with him?”

“No, Monsieur, he was quite alone.”

“Thank you, my friend. That will be all.”

Poirot turned to me with a twinkle in his eye.

“Now, Hastings, you begin to see, do you not?”

“I’m hanged if I do! What on earth are you driving at?”

“Wait until we get back to London, and I will explain all to you.”

“Ah, you mean Mr. Shaw, sir,” said the fourth steward whom we
interrogated. “Yes, he was very bad indeed, poor old gentleman.
I’m glad to see him about again.”

“He is well again?”

“Yes, sir, I’ve seen him several times in the last few days, and
he’s quite recovered. I thought at one time we should have to put
him ashore at Queenstown, he was so ill.”

Poirot drew a long breath.

“Thank you,” he said. “That is all I wanted to know.”

He turned to me with a twinkle in his eye.

“Now, Hastings, for the _dénouement_! We return to London.”

“But we haven’t found the bonds!”

“Wait, wait, _mon ami_! You should know by this time that I do not
fash myself unnecessarily!”

He hummed a little tune and refused to say another word.

On our return to London, he telephoned to Mr. Vavasour, requesting
him to meet us at his office the following morning. He also
asked Miss Farquhar and Philip Ridgeway to be present.

“That’ll be Mr. Shaw, sir,” said one of the stewards. “He was very
bad indeed, most of the way over. He had to be carried on and off.”

“Exactly,” said Poirot, his eyes twinkling. “He had a very bad
throat, eh? He could hardly speak?”

“Yes, sir. He seemed to have lost his voice almost entirely.”

“Thank you, my friend. You have been most helpful.”

He turned to me as we went down the gangway again.

“Well, Hastings? Are you still in the dark?”

“I don’t understand,” I confessed. “What on earth has the joint
manager of the Bank, Mr. Shaw, to do with it? He wasn’t even on
the boat! He was at home with bronchitis.”

“Exactly!” said Poirot, with a grin. “He was at home with
bronchitis. Or was he? That is the question. The steward says he
crossed on the boat. Mr. Vavasour says he was at home in bed.
Which is right?”

“But I saw him myself in the Bank on Friday,” I protested.

“Quite so. You saw him in the Bank on Friday. But where was he on the
Tuesday before that? When the _Olympia_ sailed? He was not at the
Bank that day, anyway.”

“He might have been at home,” I suggested. “But even so—if he had
shipped as a passenger, how did he get the bonds? Philip Ridgeway
had them in his trunk.”

“Precisely. He had them in his trunk. And the trunk was in his
cabin. And the cabin—was it not next to Mr. Shaw’s?”

“I don’t know,” I said.

“Well, I do. It was. And now, Hastings, we will return to London,
and have a little talk with the gentleman in question.”

We reached London late that evening. Early next morning we drove
to the Bank. Mr. Shaw was in his room as usual. He looked up with
some surprise as we entered.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot? Any news of the bonds?”

“A little, Monsieur Shaw. I have just returned from Liverpool.”

“From Liverpool? What took you there?”

“I have been interviewing some of the stewards on the _Olympia_.”

Mr. Shaw’s face changed slightly.

“Indeed? And what did you learn?”

“I learnt that a certain Mr. Shaw—an elderly gentleman with a
bad throat—crossed on her to New York on the 23rd.”

There was a silence. Mr. Shaw sat quite still. His face was very
pale.

“Well?” he said at last. “What of it?”

“Only this,” said Poirot, leaning forward and speaking very
distinctly. “That Mr. Shaw—the passenger—was not you, Monsieur
Shaw. He was an impostor. But he was an impostor who knew a great
deal. He knew, for instance, exactly where those bonds were
hidden. He knew more—he had a key that would open the trunk.”

“A key? But you said just now there were only three keys in
existence, and that they were all accounted for.”

“Exactly. One was with Mr. Ridgeway. The other two were in the
safe here. But—were they? You were away, Monsieur Shaw. You were
ill for a fortnight. During that time, who had access to your key?”

“No one. It was in my private safe at home.”

“Are you sure of that? Was there no one who could have got at it?
Some one who lived in the same house—some one you trusted?”

Mr. Shaw did not answer. He seemed to be thinking deeply.

“Let us go back a little,” said Poirot. “The bonds were stolen on
the _Olympia_. They were sold in New York within half an hour of
her arrival. That means the thief must have had them on him when
he landed. But every passenger was searched. How did he manage it?
There is only one way. He didn’t land with them. He—or rather his
accomplice—had already landed with them.”

“His accomplice?”

“Yes. Think, Monsieur Shaw. The _Olympia_ is a very fast boat.
But there is another boat—a smaller, older boat—that sails two
days earlier and reaches New York only a few hours after the
_Olympia_. Suppose the bonds were not on the _Olympia_ at all?
Suppose they were on that other boat? Suppose they had been
stolen, not on the high seas, but here in London—on the very
morning they were supposed to be packed?”

“But they were packed!” cried Mr. Shaw. “I saw them myself. I helped
to count them. They were put into the package and the package was
sealed and put into the trunk.”

“You saw a package put into the trunk,” corrected Poirot. “But was
it the package of bonds? You did not see them after they were
sealed, I think? You did not see them actually placed in the
trunk?”

“No—no—I suppose I didn’t. Vavasour put them in.”

“Exactly. Mr. Vavasour put them in. And Mr. Vavasour had a key.
Mr. Vavasour is Philip Ridgeway’s uncle. He knew his nephew’s
movements. He knew all about the bonds. And it was Mr. Vavasour
who had been so over-worked during your absence—so over-worked
that he might well have found time for a little—shall we say,
private business?”

“Vavasour!” gasped Mr. Shaw. “You mean Vavasour stole them?”

“I am sure of it,” said Poirot quietly. “It was a very clever
plot. The bonds were never on the _Olympia_ at all. They were
sent over to New York by the other boat, two days earlier. The
theft on the _Olympia_ was a blind—a very cleverly arranged
blind to divert suspicion and to make it seem that the bonds
had been stolen at sea. The scratches on the lock, the attempted
robbery—all that was part of the plan. And the man who crossed
as ‘Mr. Shaw’—he was an accomplice, of course, probably some
confidential clerk whom Vavasour could trust. He was there to
give colour to the story, to make it seem that you, Monsieur
Shaw, were the thief, in case things went wrong.”

Mr. Shaw sat as if turned to stone.

“Vavasour!” he whispered. “I can’t believe it. Vavasour!”

“It is hard to believe, I know,” said Poirot. “But the facts speak
for themselves. And now, Monsieur Shaw, I think we had better go
and find Mr. Vavasour. I have a little surprise for him.”

He rose and led the way out of the room. We followed him in
silence. I was too stunned to speak. Vavasour! The quiet,
respectable Bank manager! It seemed incredible. And yet, as Poirot
had said, the facts were there.

We found Mr. Vavasour in his room. He looked up as we entered, and
something in Poirot’s face must have warned him, for he turned
deadly pale.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot?” he said, and his voice shook a little.
“What is it?”

“It is the end, Monsieur Vavasour,” said Poirot gravely. “The game
is up. I know everything.”

Vavasour did not speak. He shrank back in his chair, his eyes
fixed on Poirot’s face with a look of agony.

“The bonds,” said Poirot. “Where are they?”

Vavasour made a desperate effort to recover himself.

“I—I don’t know what you mean,” he stammered. “The bonds—they
were stolen—on the _Olympia_——”

“No,” said Poirot. “They were never on the _Olympia_. You know
that as well as I do. They were stolen here—by you.”

With a cry of despair, Vavasour collapsed. His head fell forward
on his desk, and he broke into bitter sobbing.

“It’s true!” he gasped. “I did it! I was in difficulties—I needed
the money—I thought I could replace it—but it was too late—too
late——”

Poirot looked at him with a kind of pitying contempt.

“It is always too late,” he said. “And now, Monsieur Vavasour, I
think you had better come with us. There is a gentleman from
Scotland Yard waiting outside.”

As we led the broken man away, I looked at Poirot. He was
standing with his head slightly on one side, a look of modest
satisfaction on his face.

“Well, Hastings?” he said. “What do you think of my ‘childishly
simple’ case now?”

“I think you’re a marvel, Poirot,” I said. “Simply a marvel.”

Poirot smiled.

“It is the little grey cells, my friend,” he said. “The little grey
cells! They never fail one—if one knows how to use them!”

And with a flourish of his cane, he led the way out into the
bright morning sunshine of Threadneedle Street.

I was amazed at Poirot’s perseverance. He would have done credit
to a trained sleuth-hound. He visited half a dozen cabins before
he was satisfied. Finally, we were shown into one on the upper
deck, which appeared to have been occupied by an elderly gentleman
of the name of Mr. Shaw.

“You see, Hastings?” said Poirot, when we were once more on the
quay. “There is the cabin—No. 47—where the invalid lived for six
days. He was so ill that he was seen by nobody but the doctor and
his own steward.”

“And what of it?” I asked, still in the dark.

“What of it? Why, _mon ami_, do you not see?”

“I do not.”

Poirot sighed.

“I was right! You are a person of a most singular density,
Hastings!”

“Then tell me, what have we found?”

“We have found that Mr. Shaw was on board the _Olympia_!”

“Mr. Shaw! But he was in London, ill with bronchitis!”

“So he said. But who saw him?”

“His colleague, Mr. Vavasour.”

“No, Mr. Vavasour said he had not seen him for a fortnight. He
had been away from the Bank.”

“But the doctor! The ship’s doctor!”

“The ship’s doctor saw a man with a heavy beard and large tinted
spectacles, who stayed in his bunk and complained of a cough.
Wait, Hastings, and you shall see.”

“Then it was Shaw who stole the bonds?”

“It was Shaw who was on board the _Olympia_,” said Poirot
guardedly. “As to who stole the bonds—well, let us return to
London.”

The description appeared to tally with one Mr. Ventnor who had
occupied the cabin C 24 which was next to that of Philip Ridgeway.
Although unable to see how Poirot had deduced Mr. Ventnor’s
existence and personal appearance, I was keenly excited.

“Tell me,” I cried, “was this gentleman one of the first to land
when you got to New York?” The steward shook his head.

“No, indeed, sir, he was one of the last off the boat.”

I retired crestfallen, and observed Poirot grinning at me. He
thanked the steward, a note changed hands, and we took our
departure.

“It’s all very well,” I remarked heatedly, “but that last answer
must have damped your precious theory, grin as you please!”

“As usual, you see nothing, Hastings. That last answer is, on the
contrary, the coping-stone of my theory.”

I flung up my hands in despair.

“I give it up.”
