When we were in the train, speeding towards London, Poirot wrote
busily for a few minutes, sealing up the result in an envelope.

He addressed it to the joint general managers of the London and Scottish Bank. “And now, my friend,” he said, “we will have a little dinner, and then to bed. To-morrow morning we shall visit the city and see if my little bait has been swallowed. It is a case that requires the logic, the order, and the method. To-morrow, the comedy will be played out to its conclusion.”

“There, that is done,” he said, with a sigh of satisfaction. “Now,
Hastings, we go straight to the Bank. I have much to say to Mr.
Vavasour and Mr. Shaw. I think we shall find them both there.”
On our arrival, we were at once shown into the private room of
the joint managers. We found not only the two managers, but also
Philip Ridgeway and Miss Farquhar. Poirot looked round him with
an air of satisfaction.

“Take this to the London and Scottish Bank, Hastings,” he said, handing me the envelope. “Ask to see Mr. Vavasour and Mr. Shaw together. Tell them it contains the name of the person who stole the bonds. I myself have a small matter to attend to at Scotland Yard, but I shall join you at the Bank in less than an hour. Do not, I beg of you, lose that envelope, for it contains the fruit of my little grey cells!”

“To the Inspector McNeil,” he explained. “But I have also sent a
telegram to Mr. Vavasour. I have requested a meeting at the Bank
this afternoon. We shall find there, I hope, the solution to our
little problem. You see, Hastings, it is all a matter of the ‘little
grey cells.’ The facts were there for anyone to see, but it requires
the order and the method to arrange them in their proper sequence.”

On our return to London, Poirot immediately arranged a meeting at the London and Scottish Bank for the following morning. When we arrived, the atmosphere was thick with tension. Mr. Vavasour and Mr. Shaw were seated at their desks, while Philip Ridgeway and Esmée Farquhar stood by the window. Poirot greeted them all with a grave bow, then, with a theatrical gesture, he placed the sealed envelope he had been carrying on the table between the two managers. “Messieurs, Mademoiselle,” he began, “the mystery of the million dollar bonds is a mystery no longer. I have here the name of the person who staged this most ingenious drama.”

“This is for the good Inspector McNeil. We will leave it at Scotland
Yard in passing, and then to the Rendezvous Restaurant, where I
have asked Miss Esmée Farquhar to do us the honour of dining with
us.”

“What about Ridgeway?”

“What about him?” asked Poirot with a twinkle.

“Why, you surely don’t think—you can’t——”

“Patience, Hastings, patience! All will be clear in good time!”

Miss Farquhar was awaiting us, her face very pale and her hands
shaking.

“What news, Monsieur Poirot?” she asked.

“News of the best, Mademoiselle. I have sent the name of the thief
to Scotland Yard.”

“Who was it? Was it Philip?”

“Philip?” Poirot’s eyebrows went up. “Philip? No, it was not
Philip.”

“Oh, thank God! Thank God!”

The poor girl burst into a passion of tears.

“But who was it?” she sobbed.

“Do you not know, Mademoiselle? It was Mr. Shaw.”

“Mr. Shaw! But he was ill in bed!”

“Exactly!” said Poirot, with an air of immense satisfaction. “That
is why he was the only possible person who could have done it!”

“But how? When?”

“On the 23rd, Mademoiselle. To-morrow, I trust, his arrest will be
announced in the morning papers.”

“How did you find it out?” I asked.

“Because, Hastings, I saw that the key of the case lay in that
futile attempt to force the lock. If the thief had a key, why did
he try to force it? To make it look as if he hadn’t a key. But
suppose he _hadn’t_ a key? Then he _couldn’t_ open it at all. He
must, therefore, have had a key. But why did he try to force the
lock? Why, simply to make people think that he hadn’t one!”

“Mon ami, we shall see! Have I not told you that the case is
perfectly simple?”

The Rendezvous was a small but excellent restaurant in the Soho
district, and Poirot had taken the trouble to order an exceptionally
good dinner. Miss Farquhar looked charming. She was evidently
frightened and unhappy, and it was some time before Poirot’s
chatter succeeded in making her forget her anxieties. Suddenly
he said:

“Mademoiselle, what was the colour of your fiancé’s hair when he
left England on the 23rd? Was it grey at the temples?”

Miss Farquhar looked at him in surprise.

“Oh, no, Monsieur Poirot, it was quite brown.”

“Then it must have turned grey under the stress of this anxiety,
must it not?” said Poirot, with a funny little smile.

“Yes,” she said, sighing. “I’m afraid it has.”

“Wait and see, Hastings. He also is of the party.”

The restaurant was brilliantly lit, and Miss Farquhar was looking
even more charming than on our first meeting. Poirot was in his
best form, and chatted gaily. Just as the coffee arrived, Inspector
McNeil entered. He took the chair which Poirot had kept vacant for
him, and looking across at Philip Ridgeway, placed his hand on his
shoulder.

“I have a warrant for your arrest, Mr. Philip Ridgeway,” he said
gravely.

A cry broke from Esmée’s lips, and she turned a terrified face
towards Poirot.

“No, no, Monsieur Poirot, it can’t be true! Tell them it isn’t
true!”

Poirot stood up.

“One moment, Inspector. You have the papers I sent you?”

“Yes, Monsieur Poirot, I have them.”

“Then I think you will find that you have made a mistake. If you
will be so good as to accompany us to the flat of Mr. Shaw, one of
the joint general managers of the London and Scottish Bank, we may
be able to clear up this little matter.”

A taxi was summoned, and we all piled in. We were a silent and
unhappy party. Miss Farquhar was sobbing under her breath. On
arrival at Mr. Shaw’s flat, we were informed that he was at home.
He received us with some surprise.

“I am sorry to trouble you, Mr. Shaw,” said Poirot, “but we are
conducting a little experiment in connection with the theft of the
bonds. Would you be so very kind as to let us see your key of the
Hubbs’s lock?”

Mr. Shaw looked from one to the other of us. He appeared slightly
bewildered.

“Certainly, certainly,” he said, and going to a small safe in the
wall, he unlocked it and produced the key.

Poirot took it, and compared it with another which he drew from
his pocket.

“As I thought,” he said. “A duplicate. Now, Mr. Shaw, would you
mind telling us how it is that this key, which you say has never
left your possession, should be a duplicate of the one which Mr.
Ridgeway had in his portmanteau?”

Mr. Shaw’s face went white.

“I—I don’t understand,” he stammered.

“I think you do,” said Poirot. “You see, Mr. Shaw, you were not
suffering from bronchitis after all. You were on board the
_Olympia_ as Mr. Ventnor, in the cabin next to Mr. Ridgeway’s.”

A gasp of astonishment broke from us all.

“You see,” continued Poirot, “it was quite easy. You knew that
Mr. Ridgeway was taking the bonds to New York. You also knew that
he would have the key of the portmanteau with him. You had a
duplicate key made, and you also provided yourself with a set of
tools to make it appear that an attempt had been made to force the
lock. You went on board the _Olympia_ as Mr. Ventnor, and waited
your opportunity. It came when Mr. Ridgeway was at dinner. You
entered his cabin, opened the portmanteau with your duplicate key,
and took the bonds. Then you used your tools to scratch and dent
the lock, so as to make it appear that it had been forced. You
knew that a search would be made of the ship, but you also knew
that as an invalid who never left his cabin, you would be the last
person to be suspected. You stayed on board until the very last
moment, and then, when the search was over, you walked ashore with
the bonds in your pocket.”

“But the bonds were sold within half an hour of the ship’s arrival!”
cried Philip Ridgeway.

“Precisely,” said Poirot. “That was the cleverest part of the whole
scheme. You see, Mr. Shaw did not take the bonds to New York at
all. He posted them to himself—or rather to an accomplice in New
York—by the mail boat which left England two days before the
_Olympia_. The bonds were already in New York when the _Olympia_
arrived, and were sold as soon as the news of the theft was
received.”

Mr. Shaw made a sudden dash for the door, but Inspector McNeil was
too quick for him.

“I think you’d better come with me, Mr. Shaw,” he said grimly.

As the door closed behind them, Esmée Farquhar turned to Poirot,
her eyes shining with gratitude.

“Oh, Monsieur Poirot, how can we ever thank you?”

“By being happy, mademoiselle,” said Poirot, with a gallant bow.

“But how did you know, Poirot?” I asked, as we walked back to our
rooms. “How did you know that it was Mr. Shaw?”

“My friend, it was the only possible solution. Mr. Vavasour had
no motive for stealing the bonds, but Mr. Shaw—well, we found that
he had been speculating heavily, and was in urgent need of money.
Then there was the matter of the lock. As I said, if they had the
key, why waste time trying to force the lock? Only to create an
impression that the lock had been forced by some one who had not
the key. And who was likely to have a duplicate key? Only the
makers, or some one who had access to the original. Mr. Shaw had
ordered the lock, and had had the keys in his possession. The rest
was easy.”

“And Mr. Ventnor?”

“I guessed his existence from the fact that someone must have been
on board to create the necessary atmosphere of a struggle with the
lock. And who so likely as a next-door neighbour who was also an
invalid? The rest was merely a matter of confirmation.”

“Poirot,” I said, “you are a wonderful man.”

“I have often told you so, Hastings,” said Poirot, with a modest
smile. “But you are always so difficult to convince!”

“Be patient, Hastings. You will see. I have also invited Mr.
Vavasour and Mr. Shaw. They will meet us at the restaurant.”

The evening was fine and warm. Poirot’s guests were already
assembled when we arrived. Miss Farquhar looked charming in her
evening gown; Philip Ridgeway was still pale and anxious-looking.
Mr. Vavasour and Mr. Shaw were as grave and formal as ever.

“We have met,” said Poirot, “at the invitation of our charming
young friend, Miss Farquhar, to consider this little matter of the
disappearance of the Liberty Bonds. As I told you, Hastings, the
case is simple—childishly simple.”

He smiled at our expectant faces.

“First,” he continued, “let us consider the question of the lock.
As Mr. Ridgeway said, it was a special lock and therefore it could
not be opened without the key or a duplicate. And yet it was
opened—after an attempt to force it had failed. Why was that
attempt made? To show that it was a thief from outside? But if the
thief had the key, why should he bother to try and force the lock?”

He paused.

“The answer is that the thief _did not_ have the key.”

“But he opened it!” cried Ridgeway.

“Precisely. He opened it. How? With the key.”

“I don’t follow,” said Mr. Vavasour. “You say he had not the key
and yet he opened it with the key.”

“Precisely,” said Poirot, with a little bow. “He had not the key
_when he began_ to force the lock, but he had it _when he finished_.”

“Where did he get it?”

“From the person who had it—from Mr. Ridgeway.”

“But I tell you I never let it out of my possession!” cried
Ridgeway.

“I know. And yet the thief got it. How? By the simple process of
taking it from your pocket, opening the trunk, and putting the key
back again.”

“But I should have felt him!”

“Not if you were asleep—or drugged.”

“Drugged?”

“Yes, drugged.”

“But who could have drugged me?”

“The person who was in the cabin next to yours—Mr. Ventnor.”

“But I never saw him!”

“Exactly. He was an invalid, and never left his cabin. But he had
a steward, and he could easily have managed to put something into
your drink or your food.”

“But who was Mr. Ventnor?”

“Ah! that is the point. Who was Mr. Ventnor? He was a gentleman
of about sixty, with a short white beard and glasses. He was also,
I may add, a very good actor.”

Poirot’s eyes were fixed on Mr. Vavasour. The latter’s face turned
a curious grey colour.

“What—what do you mean?” he stammered.

“I mean,” said Poirot, “that Mr. Ventnor and Mr. Vavasour are one
and the same person!”

There was a moment of absolute silence. Then Mr. Vavasour spoke.

“It is a lie! A monstrous lie!”

“Is it?” said Poirot. “I think not. You see, Mr. Vavasour, I have
been making inquiries. I find that you were absent from the Bank
on the 23rd—the day the _Olympia_ sailed. You said you were ill,
but I find that you were seen at Liverpool. I also find that you
returned to London on the 28th—the day the _Olympia_ reached New
York. It was a very quick trip, was it not? You went over as Mr.
Ventnor, and you came back as—well, you did not come back on the
_Olympia_.”

“But the bonds?” cried Ridgeway. “How did he get them ashore?”

“He did not get them ashore,” said Poirot. “He sent them by post.”

“By post?”

“Yes. He posted them to himself—or rather to an accomplice—in New
York. That is why they were sold so soon after the _Olympia_ docked.
The mail boat, which left Liverpool on the same day as the _Olympia_,
reached New York some hours before her. The bonds were there
waiting for him.”

Mr. Vavasour made a sudden movement, but Poirot was too quick for
him.

“No, no, Mr. Vavasour. It is no use. The police are outside. I
think you had better go quietly.”

The door opened and Inspector McNeil entered.

“Mr. Vavasour,” he said, “I have a warrant for your arrest on a
charge of stealing a million dollars’ worth of Liberty Bonds, the
property of the London and Scottish Bank.”

Mr. Vavasour stood for a moment, his face working. Then he turned
and followed the Inspector out of the room.

Miss Farquhar went up to Philip Ridgeway and put her hand in his.

“Oh, Philip!” she whispered. “I am so glad!”

Philip Ridgeway looked at Poirot.

“I don’t know how to thank you, Monsieur Poirot,” he said. “You
have saved my reputation—and my happiness.”

“It was nothing,” said Poirot, with a modest wave of his hand. “A
little matter of deduction—that is all.”

“But how did you know?” I asked, as we walked back to our rooms.
“How did you know it was Vavasour?”

“It was the lock, Hastings. The lock was the clue. It was a special
lock, and only three people had the keys—Mr. Ridgeway, Mr. Vavasour,
and Mr. Shaw. Now, if the thief had been an outsider, he would
have had to have a duplicate key. But to get a duplicate key, he
would have had to have the original. And who could have given it
to him? Only one of the three people who held the keys.

“Now, I did not think it was Mr. Ridgeway. He had no motive. He
was a trusted official of the Bank, and he was engaged to a very
charming girl. I did not think it was Mr. Shaw. He was ill at the
time. That left Mr. Vavasour.

“And when I began to look into Mr. Vavasour’s movements, I found
that he had been absent from the Bank on the 23rd. That was enough
for me. The rest was easy.”

“But why did he do it?”

“Ah! that I do not know. Perhaps he had been speculating. Perhaps
he was in debt. Who knows? But he was a clever man, Hastings. A
very clever man. If it had not been for Hercule Poirot, he would
have succeeded.”

He sighed.

“It is a great responsibility, Hastings, to be so gifted. But one
must do one’s best—one must do one’s best!”

“What I think—or do not think—is not yet to be said. But I observe,
Hastings, that your thoughts run on a certain track. Is it because
he is a handsome young man, and has a very charming fiancée, that
your heart bleeds for him?”

I did not answer. Miss Farquhar was awaiting us, looking more
beautiful than ever. Poirot was at his most gallant. We were half-way
through our dinner when he suddenly looked up and nodded to some
one who was passing.

“Aha! Here is our friend, the Inspector McNeil.”

The Inspector, a tall, silent man, drew a chair to the table and
sat down. Poirot leaned forward and spoke in a low voice.

“Well?”

The Inspector nodded.

“The search has been made, Monsieur Poirot. Every point of yours
has been verified.”

“Everything?”

“Everything.”

“The habit of incoherence is growing upon you, Hastings. As a
matter of fact I _did_ think. If Ridgeway had been the thief—which
was perfectly possible—the case would have been charming; a piece
of neat methodical work.”

“But not so charming for Miss Farquhar.”

“Ah, well, one must take these things into account. But I was not
mistaken in her, she is a girl of some intelligence, and she was
quick enough to suspect—well, never mind who she suspected. Here
she is!”

I looked up to see Esmée Farquhar standing by the door of the
Rendezvous. Her face was very pale, and she was trembling.

“You have found the thief, Monsieur Poirot?” she asked.

“Yes, mademoiselle.”

“And it is——” She broke off, her eyes fixed on his face.

“It is Mr. Shaw!” said Poirot quietly.

I gave a gasp of surprise. Mr. Shaw! The joint general manager!
The man who had been ill!

“He and no other,” Poirot said. “It was a very clever plot, and
highly ingenious. Mr. Shaw is a man of large and varied
attainments. He is a good actor, a good makeup artist, and he is
a man of no little physical activity. He was ‘ill’ for a fortnight,
you remember. During that time, he was on board the _Olympia_ in
the character of the invalid Mr. Ventnor.”

“Exactly. I take it she is a young lady of some character and
decision. She would probably have remained at his side until the
last, and even after—if it were a first offence. But we must have
charity—even for the thief. Let us think of him as someone who
has been tempted beyond his strength, someone who saw a golden
opportunity and could not resist it.”

“One of the managers?” I asked, in a whisper.

Poirot nodded.

“One of them—yes.”

“Vavasour or Shaw?”

“The one who stayed at home? Or the one who was away? It was a
cleverly thought-out scheme, Hastings. The bonds were never on
the _Olympia_ at all!”

“But Ridgeway saw them put into the trunk!”

“He saw a package, my friend, which he _believed_ contained the
bonds. They were already in America, having been sent by the
previous mail.”

“Then who was the invalid in the next cabin?”

“A very necessary person. He was there to provide the ‘clues’—the
scratched lock, the ‘attempt’ to force the trunk. He was, in fact,
the thief’s confederate.”

“And the thief?”

“The thief, Hastings, was the man who had the opportunity to send
the bonds to America beforehand, and who then staged the ‘theft’
on the _Olympia_ to cover his tracks.”

“Shaw!” I cried. “He was away for a fortnight with ‘bronchitis’!”

“Exactly. ‘Bronchitis’ is a very convenient malady. It allows one
to be away from the office, and yet—if one is careful—not
necessarily confined to one’s bed. A little make-up, a pair of
spectacles, a muffled voice—and Mr. Shaw becomes Mr. Ventnor,
occupying the cabin next to his unsuspecting nephew.”

“But the bonds were sold within half an hour of the _Olympia’s_
arrival!”

“Precisely. Because they were already there, waiting for the
signal. As soon as the _Olympia_ was sighted, the confederate in
New York—who had been warned by cable—began to sell. The ‘theft’
on board was discovered just as the ship docked, providing the
perfect alibi.”

“And the key?”

“Mr. Shaw had his own key, of course. He didn't need to force the
lock—he only had to make it _look_ as though someone had tried to.”

“It’s incredible!” I exclaimed. “A man in his position!”

“The ‘easy’ cases are often the most surprising, Hastings. But
here is the Rendezvous. Let us see if Miss Farquhar has arrived.”

Miss Farquhar was waiting for us, and I was again struck by her
delicate beauty and the perfection of her self-possession. Poirot
shook her by the hand.

“Well, mademoiselle,” he said, “I have to tell you that I have
solved your little problem.”

“You have found the thief? Oh, Monsieur Poirot, how can I ever
thank you?”

“It was simple, mademoiselle, quite simple! You remember that the
bonds were offered for sale half an hour _before_ the _Olympia_
docked in New York?”

“Yes, it seemed so extraordinary.”

“Not at all. The bonds were never on the _Olympia_.”

“But they were! Philip saw them put in the trunk and locked!”

“He _thought_ he did.”

“But—I don’t understand.”

“I will explain. On the morning of the 23rd, Mr. Vavasour and Mr.
Shaw were alone in their office. They were expecting Mr. Ridgeway.
They had the bonds there. Also they had a duplicate trunk—an exact
replica of the one Mr. Shaw had had made for Mr. Ridgeway.
Into this duplicate they put, not the bonds, but a quantity of
worthless paper. When Mr. Ridgeway arrived, the first trunk—the
real one—was already locked and sealed. It was the _duplicate_
trunk which was then opened and shown to him. He saw the bonds
being put in, the trunk was locked and he was given the key. He
took that trunk to the _Olympia_.”

“But—the real bonds?”

“They were sent over to New York by the faster boat, the _Gigantic_,
which sailed on the same day as the _Olympia_, but from Southampton.
The _Gigantic_ arrived in New York some hours before the _Olympia_.”

“But why—why should they do such a thing?”

“Because, mademoiselle, one of those two ‘stodgy’ old gentlemen
was a very clever and daring thief. He had use for a million
dollars. He knew that the theft would be discovered as soon as the
_Olympia_ docked. He needed someone to be the scapegoat. Who
better than his nephew, or his colleague’s nephew? He had the
duplicate trunk made, he even went to the trouble of having the
lock of the first trunk tampered with on board the _Olympia_ so as
to suggest a theft during the voyage. He himself—the thief—took
the real bonds to New York on the _Gigantic_.”

“But which of them? Which of them was it?”

“It was the one who was ‘taken ill’ with bronchitis on the very day
that the _Olympia_ sailed. He was ‘ill’ in a hotel in New York!
The description of the invalid Mr. Ventnor, who occupied the cabin
next to Mr. Ridgeway, and who was one of the last to leave the
ship, was a masterpiece of misdirection. Mr. Shaw, in short, was
the thief.”

“But—the keys?”

“He had his own key, of course. He only had to wait for a
favourable moment to slip into Ridgeway’s cabin and tamper with the
lock of the duplicate trunk. He knew it could not be opened. Then,
having done that, he had only to wait for the _Gigantic_ to
arrive, and for the _Olympia_ to follow. He had already sold the
bonds through his agents in New York before the _Olympia_ docked.”

“And Philip—is he cleared?”

“I have just left a full account of the matter with Inspector
McNeil. He will, I imagine, lose no time in acting upon it.”

“Oh, Monsieur Poirot, I don’t know how to thank you!”

“It was a very pretty little problem,” said Poirot, “but, as I
told Hastings, it was almost too easy. The duplicate trunk was the
clue. Once I had realized that the bonds could not have been
stolen on the _Olympia_, the rest followed as a matter of course.”

“And now,” I said, “let us have dinner.”

“Ah, no. The girl! She is very pretty, Hastings. I saw you looking
at her with much interest—and I myself am not so old as to be
insensible to a beautiful woman. To please her we will give
McNeil his chance.”

The Rendezvous was a small, well-managed restaurant in Soho, where
Poirot was well known. We arrived early, and it was not until half
an hour later that Miss Farquhar arrived, looking more charming
than ever in a simple evening gown. She looked around with a
certain amount of anxiety.

“Philip?” she asked. “Is he not here? I—I thought he would be
dining with us.”

“Aha! Miss Farquhar, you will have to put up with our dull company
this evening, I am afraid. But see, here is someone you know.”

Inspector McNeil of Scotland Yard was coming towards us.

“Good evening, Inspector,” said Poirot. “I hope your little
surprise is a success.”

McNeil nodded.

“It’s a success all right, Monsieur Poirot, thanks to you. We’ve
got our man. He was trying to catch the midnight express to the
North.”

Miss Farquhar turned as white as a sheet.

“Who—who is it?” she gasped. “Philip? Oh, no, not Philip!”

“It’s not Mr. Ridgeway, miss,” said the Inspector kindly. “It’s
one of the big men of the Bank—Mr. Shaw, in fact.”

Miss Farquhar gave a little cry and sank into her chair.

“Mr. Shaw!” she repeated. “But he was ill—he was away from the
Bank!”

“_Eh bien_, you are a sentimentalist. But do not fear for her.
The thief is not her Philip.”

“Who is it, then?”

“Did I not say we would have dinner?”

Miss Farquhar was already there. She looked pale and anxious, and
it was clear that she was findng it difficult to force an interest
in the _hors d’œuvres_ and the excellent soup.

“Is there any news, Monsieur Poirot?” she asked. “You have been
to Liverpool?”

“Yes, Mademoiselle.”

“And you have found—the thief?”

“I have.”

“Who was it? Was it—was it Philip?”

Poirot smiled.

“No, Mademoiselle, it was not Philip. He was the tool, the
unconscious tool, of a very clever man. But even the cleverest
have their little weaknesses. His was—how shall I say it?—a
longing for a sea-voyage!”

“A sea-voyage?” Miss Farquhar stared.

“Precisely. You will remember, Mademoiselle, that Mr. Shaw was
ill—_très malade_, with bronchitis—at the time of the sailing of
the _Olympia_.”

“Yes.”

“And that Mr. Vavasour was at the Bank?”

“Yes.”

“And yet, Mademoiselle, it was Mr. Shaw who went to New York on
the _Olympia_.”

I let out a whistle.

“Shaw!” I cried. “But how on earth——”

“My dear friend, do not forget the description given us by the
steward. An elderly gentleman, wearing glasses, a great invalid,
who hardly moved out of his cabin. A wig, a pair of spectacles,
and the thing is done. He takes the cabin next to that of Philip
Ridgeway, and has the key of the Hubbs’s lock in his pocket. It is
child’s play for him to go into Ridgeway’s cabin when the latter
is at dinner, and with his own key unlock the trunk and take the
bonds. Then, as a refinement, he tries to force the lock, to give
it the appearance of a common thief’s work. He goes to New York,
and before the _Olympia_ has even docked, the bonds have been sold.
Of course, he stays in his cabin until the last possible moment,
and then slips off, gets into a taxi, and catches the next boat
back to England.”

“But how could he?” I cried. “His partner——”

“His partner was too busy to think of anything else but his work,
and he had no reason to suspect his colleague. Mr. Shaw, in fact,
remained in bed—with a doctor and a nurse—at his own house.”

“But the doctor and the nurse?” I persisted.

“The doctor and the nurse were easily managed. A little money,
and a little—how shall I say it?—_chantage_? No, I think it was
simply a matter of hiring a couple of actors to play the parts.
And, of course, the real Mr. Shaw was on the _Olympia_ all the
time.”

“But why—why did he do it?” asked Miss Farquhar.

“Ah, Mademoiselle, a Bank manager is not always the ‘keen financier
with an eagle glance’ that the novels describe. Sometimes he is
a man who has made a series of unfortunate investments, and who
sees ruin staring him in the face. And then, he sees a million
dollars’ worth of Liberty Bonds, and—_voilà!_”

“But Philip?” asked Miss Farquhar. “What will happen to him?”

“Oh, Philip will be all right. The Bank will be only too glad to
hush the matter up, and Philip will find himself in a very strong
position. And, of course, he will have his Esmée to console him!”

Poirot smiled at the girl, who was now blushing and looking very
happy.

“And now,” said Poirot, “let us enjoy our dinner!”

“Possibly you are right. Therefore all is for the best. Now,
Hastings, let us review the case. I can see that you are dying to
do so. The sealed package is removed from the trunk and vanishes,
as Miss Farquhar puts it, into thin air. We will dismiss the thin
air theory, which is not practicable at the present stage of
science, and consider what is likely to have become of it. Every
one asserts the incredibility of its being smuggled ashore——”

“Yes, but we know——”

“We know nothing, Hastings. We only guess. Suppose, for instance,
that the bonds were never in the trunk at all? That they were never
on the _Olympia_?”

“But I thought——”

“You thought—yes, exactly. You did not observe. You did not see
the clue of the Hubbs’s lock—it was that which first gave me the
key to the situation.”

“I don’t understand.”

“Wait. To-night all will be made clear.”

But it was not until we were seated at dinner with Miss Farquhar
that the mystery was finally solved. Philip Ridgeway joined us,
still looking worn and anxious, but Poirot’s first words
electrified us.

“Hush! let me continue my little lecture. Now, if it was not
smuggled ashore, what follows? That it was already ashore! And how
could it be already ashore? Why, by never having been on board!
That is the only way of getting out of the difficulty.”

I stared.

“But the bonds were seen to be put into the trunk.”

“By whom? By Mr. Vavasour and Mr. Shaw. They are the only witnesses.
Therefore, if the bonds were never on board, one of these two
gentlemen must have been the thief.”

“But they were both there!”

“Precisely. That is the beauty of it. To all appearance they were
both there. But let us examine the facts. Mr. Shaw, we are told,
has been ill with bronchitis since the 23rd—the day the _Olympia_
sailed. He was not there to see his colleague off. He was not there
to see his nephew off. In fact, he was not there at all!”

“Then who was the person whom Ridgeway saw?”

“Can you not guess? Mr. Vavasour, of course! He is a man of sixty,
with a beard. It is not difficult to ‘make up’ as a man of sixty
with a beard, if one is, say, thirty, and has a certain amount of
histrionic ability. Mr. Ridgeway, you remember, is thirty, and has
a touch of grey at the temples. He is also a ‘trusted official’
of the bank, which means that he is well known to the customers,
and his appearance is familiar.”

“But his uncle?”

“His uncle, Mr. Vavasour, was also in the plot. It was he who
suggested his nephew for the mission. It was he who ordered the
special lock. It was he who, with his ‘colleague,’ saw the bonds
put into the trunk. But the ‘colleague’ was his nephew, Philip
Ridgeway, in disguise!”

“Good heavens, Poirot! Do you mean to say that Ridgeway—?”

“Wait! Let us see what happens. The bonds are never put into the
trunk. Instead, Ridgeway, as himself, goes to Liverpool. But first,
as ‘Mr. Shaw,’ he has seen to it that the bonds are safely in his
own pockets. He goes on board the _Olympia_. He has with him the
duplicate key of the trunk. In the middle of the voyage, he
scratches and marks the lock, to make it look as though an attempt
had been made to force it, and then unlocks it with the key. The
bonds, of course, are not there. He raises the alarm. The ship is
searched—with no result. Naturally! The bonds are already in New
York!”

“But how?”

“By the simplest method in the world. They were posted to a
confederate in New York by the mail-boat which left two days
before the _Olympia_! That is why they were being sold within half
an hour of her arrival. The confederate had them already!”

“And Mr. Ventnor?”

“Mr. Ventnor was Philip Ridgeway again! He had a double cabin.
As Ridgeway, he was seen by everyone. As Ventnor, the invalid who
never left his cabin, he was seen by no one—except the steward.
He had only to ‘make up’ a little, and the thing was done. He
occupied the two cabins alternately. That is why the steward of
C 24 said he was one of the last to land. Ridgeway had to ‘land’
first, and then come back for his ‘invalid friend’!”

“But the bronchitis?”

“A very convenient malady! It kept the real Mr. Shaw out of the
way, while his ‘double’ was busy at the Bank and on the _Olympia_.”

“It’s incredible!” I murmured.

“It is very simple,” said Poirot. “And now, let us go and meet
Miss Farquhar. I think she will be interested in our little
theory.”

But Miss Farquhar was not at the Rendezvous Restaurant. Instead,
we found a note from her, saying that she had been ‘unavoidably
detained.’

“Aha!” said Poirot. “I think our young friend has taken the hint.
She is a very clever young woman, is Miss Esmée Farquhar. I suspect
that she and Mr. Philip Ridgeway are by this time well on their
way to—shall we say—South America?”

“Then she was in it too?” I cried.

“Of course! It was she who came to me, with that charming air of
distress, to put me on the track of the ‘thief.’ She knew that if
I investigated the case, I should eventually discover the truth.
And she also knew that, by the time I did so, they would have had
ample time to make their escape. It was a very clever move.”

“But why did she come to you at all?”

“Because, my friend, it is always better to have the great Hercule
Poirot on your side than against you! If she had not come to me,
I might have been employed by the Bank. As it was, I was her
‘private’ investigator. A very subtle distinction!”

“And the bonds?”

“Oh, the bonds are gone. But we have the satisfaction of knowing
how it was done. And that, after all, is the main thing, is it
not?”

I looked at Poirot’s beaming face, and wondered. To him, the
solution of the mystery was everything. The fact that the
criminals had escaped, and that he had been used as a cat’s-paw,
seemed to matter not at all. Truly, he was a remarkable man!

“One moment, Hastings. We know that the bonds were sold in New
York before the _Olympia_ arrived. How did they get there? The
answer is simple: they were never on the _Olympia_ at all!”

“But Ridgeway——”

“Let us take the facts in order. The package is sealed in the
presence of Ridgeway, Mr. Vavasour, and Mr. Shaw. They go to the
strong room, and from there Ridgeway takes it. He has it in his
possession for some hours before he leaves for Liverpool. Is that
not so? During that time he is at the Bank. He is an old and
trusted employee. He has every opportunity of opening the package,
removing the bonds, and substituting some waste paper of the same
weight and bulk. Then he seals it up again with the Bank seal,
which would be easy for him to do.”

“Poirot!” I cried. “You don't mean that Ridgeway—that Esmée's fiancé——”

“Do we? I said just now that the case was childishly simple. Look
at it this way. The bonds were in the trunk on the morning of the
23rd. They were sold in New York within half an hour of the
_Olympia’s_ arrival. Therefore they _must_ have been on board. How
did they get off? They didn’t. They were never on board.”

“But—the uncle and Mr. Shaw saw them——”

“No, they saw a package. They didn’t see the bonds. They counted
them, yes, and sealed them, yes. But they didn’t see the package
put into the trunk. They only saw Ridgeway put it there.”

“But Ridgeway wouldn’t——”

“Wait. Suppose that the package he put into the trunk did not
contain the bonds at all? Suppose it was a dummy? Then what
happens? The bonds were never on board. They stayed in London.
They were sent to New York by the _Mauretania_, which sails from
Southampton on the same day as the _Olympia_ from Liverpool. The
_Mauretania_ is a faster boat, and reaches New York a full day
ahead of the _Olympia_. The bonds are sold, and the thief is
safe.”

“But the trunk was forced!”

“Exactly. By the thief, to create the impression that they _had_
been on board. He must have a duplicate key. Who had a duplicate
key? The two managers. Mr. Vavasour and Mr. Shaw.”

“But Shaw was ill!”

“Was he? Or did he only say so? He was at the Bank on the 23rd,
and that was the day the _Mauretania_ sailed. He was ‘taken ill’
on that day. He could have caught the _Mauretania_ at Southampton,
reached New York, sold the bonds, and returned on the _Olympia_
as the ‘invalid Mr. Ventnor’ in the cabin next to Ridgeway’s. He
then has only to slip into Ridgeway’s cabin, which he can do
with his own duplicate key, and make a few scratches on the lock
to suggest a forced entry. He stays in his cabin until the last
moment, so that Ridgeway—who might recognize him—does not see him.
He then returns to London, and appears at the Bank as the
convalescent Mr. Shaw.”

“But the bonds—how could he have got them?”

“He and Vavasour counted them together. It would be easy for him
to substitute a dummy package of the same weight and appearance.
Vavasour, suspecting nothing, would not notice.”

“It's incredible!” I exclaimed.

“It is the only possible explanation. And here we are at the
Rendezvous, and there is Miss Farquhar waiting for us. I think,
Hastings, that we shall have some very good news for her.”

“Wait a moment, Hastings. I don’t say that the bonds _were_ smuggled
ashore. They could hardly have been. But you see, my friend, you
overlook the simplest and most obvious possibility—that the bonds
were never on the boat at all.”

“What!” I exclaimed. “But Ridgeway saw them put into the trunk.”

“He _saw_ a package which he was _told_ contained the bonds. He
did not see the bonds themselves.”

“But the two managers were there!”

“Precisely. Both of them. And one of them, Mr. Shaw, has been ill
with bronchitis for a fortnight. He was, in fact, ill on the very
day the bonds were supposed to have been packed.”

“You mean—?”

“I mean that the man who was in the office that morning was not
the real Mr. Shaw at all. He was an impostor—a very clever one,
no doubt, but an impostor nonetheless.”

“_You_ may know, Hastings. I do not. I take the view that, since
it seemed incredible, it _was_ incredible. Two possibilities
remain: it was hidden on board—also rather difficult—or it was
thrown overboard.”

“With a cork on it, do you mean?”

“Without a cork.”

I stared.

“But if the bonds were thrown overboard, they couldn’t have been
sold in New York.”

“I admire your logical mind, Hastings. The bonds were sold in New
York, therefore they were not thrown overboard. You see where that
leads us?”

“Where we were when we started.”

“Not at all. It leads us back to the Bank. The bonds were in the
Bank—the bonds were sold in New York. If they were not on the
_Olympia_ they must have gone by some other boat. What other boat?
The _Gigantic_, which sailed on the 21st, two days before the
_Olympia_!”

“But how—who could have——”

“Who, indeed? Who had the keys of the safe at the Bank? The two
joint general managers. One of them, Mr. Shaw, was taken ill—on
the very day the bonds were to be sent! A most convenient
bronchitis, which allowed him to be absent from the Bank and
secretly board the _Gigantic_ on the 21st, taking the real bonds
with him.”

“Then the package Ridgeway took——”

“Contained only brown paper, my friend! Shaw had a duplicate key
made for the trunk—he ordered the lock himself, remember—and it
was he who, in the character of the invalid Mr. Ventnor, occupied
the cabin next to Ridgeway. He it was who made those scratches on
the lock of the trunk, to make it appear that a clumsy attempt
had been made to force it, and then used his key to open it and
abstract the dummy package, which he then threw overboard through
the porthole!”

“But why did he wait until the _Olympia_ was almost at New York?”

“Because he had to be sure that the real bonds, which he had
posted to his confederate in New York on his arrival there, would
be sold before the theft was discovered. As an invalid, he could
remain in his cabin and avoid being seen by Ridgeway. His plan
was perfect—except for one thing.”

“And what was that?”

“He did not reckon on Hercule Poirot!”

“Exactly. Now we come to the crux of the matter—the lock. Philip
Ridgeway told us that when he went to his cabin he found his trunk
had been tampered with. It had been scratched and hacked about,
but not opened.”

“Well?”

“Well, Hastings, does that strike you as the work of a professional
thief? A professional thief would have gone to work differently.
He would have known that the lock was one of Hubbs’s, and would
have known also that it would have been quite impossible to pick
it. He would therefore have taken the trunk away with him, and
opened it at leisure. Why, then, this hacking and scratching? To
draw Ridgeway’s attention to the trunk? No, that is not it. It
could only have been done to make it _appear_ that some one had
tried to force the lock, and had failed.”

“But the trunk _was_ opened,” I said.

“Precisely. It was opened—and by the key.”

“Then you think that one of the two managers——”

“My dear Hastings, did I not tell you just now that the case was
simple? Let us go a step further. The bonds were sold in New York
before the _Olympia_ reached the quay. What does that suggest to
you?”

“That they were not on the _Olympia_ at all!” I cried.

“Splendid, Hastings! You are excelling yourself. They were never
on the _Olympia_. They were sold in New York while the _Olympia_
was still on the high seas. How? Because they had been sent over
by the mail boat which left four days before the _Olympia_.”

“But then the package that Ridgeway saw sealed up——”

“Contained—not bonds, but a few sheets of blank paper.”

“But who put it in the trunk?”

“The person who had the key. Either Mr. Vavasour or Mr. Shaw. Now,
Mr. Vavasour has been at the Bank every day. Mr. Shaw, on the other
hand, has been at home for a fortnight with—bronchitis.”

“Good heavens!” I said. “And the invalid, Mr. Ventnor?”

“Was Mr. Shaw, of course! He was not so ill that he could not
slip over to Liverpool, and take a passage on the _Olympia_ in an
assumed name. He had the second key. He it was who made the
scratches on the trunk and then opened it with the key, and
removed the—blank paper! Then he could wait for the ship to dock,
and stroll off at his leisure, his ‘illness’ having been well
timed to cover his absence from London. He’d already seen to it
that the real bonds were sold in New York by an agent.”

“But the search?”

“He was not searched. He was an invalid—a ‘Mr. Ventnor.’ Who would
suspect a poor old gentleman in a cabin? Besides, he had nothing
on him. The bonds were already sold.”

“Then why did he go at all?”

“To make the ‘theft’ on board the _Olympia_ a reality, and to
throw suspicion on the unfortunate Ridgeway. If the bonds were
stolen on the ship, Ridgeway would be the person to suffer. As it
is, I think I have been able to clear his name. He will be at the
Rendezvous to-night with Miss Farquhar.”

“And Shaw?”

“The good McNeil will have seen to him. He was to have returned on
the _Olympia_, you see. That’s why I was so anxious to see the
stewards. It was a very neat plan, and but for the fact that the
bonds were sold too soon, he might have carried it off.”

“Why did he do that?”

“The temptation of a sudden rise in the market, I expect. He is,
as I found out by a little inquiry, a ‘keen financier,’ and he
couldn’t resist it. He wanted to make sure of his profits. After
all, he is only human!”

“What about Mr. Vavasour?”

“Mr. Vavasour is a very honest man. He had no idea that his
colleague was a rogue. It was Shaw who suggested the new lock,
Shaw who made all the arrangements. Vavasour was merely the
cat’s-paw. He will be very much surprised when he hears the truth.”

“And so,” I said, “the mystery of the million dollar bond robbery
is solved.”

“It was never much of a mystery, Hastings. As I said, it was
childishly simple. But it has been an interesting little problem.
And now—let us go and meet Miss Farquhar and the fortunate Mr.
Ridgeway.”

“No, Hastings. It leads us to the conclusion that the bonds sold
in New York were not the bonds stolen from the _Olympia_.”

“But they were! The numbers tallied!”

“Ah! my friend, the numbers tallied! Now, Hastings, consider
another point. If _you_ were a thief, would you wait until you
got on board a ship, where you were in a small space, with your
movements strictly limited, before stealing a million dollars in
bonds? No, you would steal them before you went on board. But
then, you see, the bonds were seen by Mr. Ridgeway when he was
with the two managers of the Bank.”

“Well, then!”

“Exactly. But were they? He saw a package which he _believed_
contained the bonds. Now, Hastings, consider the lock. A very
elaborate lock, which someone tries to force, but fails, and
finally opens with a key. Why did he try to force it?”

“Because he hadn’t the key.”

“Exactly! But if he hadn’t the key, and yet opened the lock, he
must have _found_ the key! Where? In Philip Ridgeway’s pocket?
No, he would have had to pick his pocket for that, and then he
wouldn’t have tried to force the lock first. No, the key was left
in the lock.”

“Poirot, what do you mean?”

“That is what I ask myself. The key was left in the lock, and the
thief—not knowing this—tried to force the lock, failed, and then
discovered that the key was there all the time!”

“But how could it have been?”

“The person who put the package in the trunk, Hastings! He forgot
to remove the key.”

“Mr. Ridgeway?”

“No, no, he was looking on. One of the two managers. Which one?
The one who had been ill—Mr. Shaw! He was the one who had the bonds
in his possession, and who made up the package. It was he who
stole the bonds, substituted a dummy package, and then—_hélas!_—forgot
his key in the lock of the trunk. He was too ill to go to the
Bank, you remember? He was at home, ‘ill’ with bronchitis—but
really he was on the _Olympia_ as Mr. Ventnor! He had plenty of
time to dispose of the dummy package—which he did by throwing it
overboard. The real bonds were already in New York, and were being
sold by his confederates.”

“But the numbers, Poirot?”

“Numbers are easily altered, Hastings. He had all the time in the
world to do that. And then, he arrives in New York, waits until
the last moment to land—so as to be sure that the theft is
discovered and the search over—and then quietly walks off. A
very simple and elegant little crime!”

I was silent.

“But why did he try to force the lock?” I asked at last.

“Ah! that was his one mistake. He wanted it to look like a
clumsy theft by one of the stewards, and so he tried to force the
lock. He forgot that he had left his own key in it!”

“And the description?”

“I guessed that, mon ami. A man who has just had bronchitis would
naturally be an invalid and wear glasses.”

“You are a marvel, Poirot!” I cried. “But what about Miss
Farquhar?”

“Ah! she will be very happy, for her lover’s name will be cleared.
And now, let us go and meet her at the Rendezvous.”

As we drove along, I could not help thinking how right Poirot had
been. It _was_ a simple case, after all—to a mind like his.

“Not at all. It leads us to the fact that the bonds were _never
stolen at all_—on the _Olympia_.”

“But they were!”

“No, no, Hastings. Only the _package_ which was supposed to
contain them was stolen. The bonds were never in the package. It
was a dummy, containing only some old newspapers of no value.”

I stared at him in amazement.

“Then—the bonds were never sent at all?”

“Exactly.”

“But who—who——”

“Who, but one of the two men who had charge of them and who alone
could have put them into the package? One of them, Mr. Shaw, has
been ill with ‘bronchitis’—a very convenient malady!—ever since
the 23rd. The other, Mr. Vavasour, is a man of the highest
integrity.”

“Then it must have been Shaw!” I cried. “But how did he manage to
get the dummy package stolen?”

“That is what puzzled me for a time. But then it occurred to me
that, if Ridgeway were the thief, he would naturally make it
appear that someone else had broken into his trunk. He would want
to make it as realistic as possible—hence the scratches on the
lock. But if someone else were the thief—say Mr. Shaw—he would
want the theft to be discovered as soon as possible, in order to
divert suspicion from himself. He would want it to appear that
the theft had taken place on the _Olympia_. What easier than for
him to go to Liverpool, and, disguised as an invalid, occupy the
cabin next to Ridgeway’s? He could easily slip into Ridgeway’s
cabin when the latter was at dinner, and with the duplicate key
which he possessed, open the trunk and remove the dummy package.”

“But the scratches on the lock?”

“Ah, those were a stroke of genius on Shaw’s part! He knew that
Ridgeway would be the first to be suspected, and he wanted to make
it appear that Ridgeway himself had tried to force the lock, in
order to make it look as if someone else had done it! A very
pretty piece of work, Hastings!”

“And the bonds?”

“Oh, those he had already disposed of in London, before the
_Olympia_ sailed. He had several days’ start, you see.”

“But why did he wait until the _Olympia_ reached New York before
selling them there?”

“He didn’t. He sold them in London, to a broker who had
connections in New York. The broker then cabled his New York
correspondent to sell them as soon as the _Olympia_ docked. It
was all very neatly arranged.”

“And the description of the invalid?”

“I guessed that, of course. It was the only way he could have
managed it. And the steward’s description confirmed my guess.”

“Well, Poirot, I must hand it to you! You’ve done it again!”

“It was simple, Hastings, simple! As I said, a mere matter of
the little grey cells!”

We reached the Rendezvous Restaurant just as Miss Farquhar arrived.
Poirot greeted her with his usual gallantry, and as we sat down to
dinner, he told her the whole story.

She listened in silence, her eyes fixed on his face. When he had
finished, she drew a long breath.

“And Philip? What will happen to him?”

“He will be completely exonerated, Mademoiselle. I have already
informed the Bank and Scotland Yard. Mr. Shaw will be arrested
to-night.”

“Oh, Monsieur Poirot, how can I ever thank you?”

“By being happy, Mademoiselle. That is the best thanks you can
give me.”

And as we raised our glasses to toast the young couple, I couldn’t
help thinking that, once again, the little grey cells of Hercule
Poirot had triumphed over the most baffling of mysteries.

“No, indeed. Since the bonds were sold in New York, they must
have reached New York. If they were not on the _Olympia_, they must
have reached New York by some other means. And as they were sold
even _before_ the _Olympia_ arrived, it follows that they reached
New York _before_ the _Olympia_. Now, how could they do that? Not
by any other boat, for there were none. Therefore they must have
gone by the _Olympia_ herself. But they were not on her! We are
in a vicious circle, Hastings. We must start again. Let us go
back to the Bank. The bonds are handed over to Philip Ridgeway.
By whom? By the two joint general managers. One of them, Mr. Shaw,
was taken ill on that very day, and remained away from the Bank
for a fortnight. That is a very important fact, Hastings. It
suggests to my mind a very simple solution. What if the bonds
were never in the package at all?”

“Poirot!”

“It is so simple! The package is prepared. Mr. Shaw is taken ill.
The package is handed to Ridgeway. But it does not contain the
bonds! They are already on their way to New York, having been
despatched by the previous mail-boat.”

“But the seals?”

“Ah! the seals! They were made in the presence of Ridgeway. But
who made them? Mr. Shaw. And Mr. Shaw, you will remember, had had
a special lock fitted to the portmanteau, and also held one of
the keys. He was also the person who would naturally be in charge
of the bonds.”

“_Jamais de la vie!_ If the package was thrown overboard, and the
bonds were sold in New York, the package could not have contained
the bonds. Is there any evidence that the package _did_ contain
the bonds? Remember, Mr. Ridgeway never opened it from the time it
was placed in his hands in London.”

“Yes, but then——”

Poirot waved an impatient hand.

“Wait, I will finish. Now, we will consider the second half of
your question: how were the bonds sold in New York? The bonds were
in London, you say. Then they must have been sent to New York, and
not by the _Olympia_. How then? By the mail boat which left
Southampton on the 23rd, the _Mauretania_. And since the bonds were
in New York _before_ the _Olympia_ arrived, they must have been
posted in London on the 22nd, or early on the 23rd.”

“But they were handed over to Ridgeway on the 23rd!”

“By whom?”

“By the two managers.”

“Exactly. Now, we will look at those two managers. Mr. Vavasour
and Mr. Shaw. They both had keys to the trunk. One of them, Mr.
Shaw, had the lock made. He was also conveniently ill for a
fortnight. What would be easier than for him to have a duplicate
key made, and, after the bonds were sealed up, to substitute a
dummy package, and then to post the real bonds to New York to an
accomplice? He would then wait for his colleague to be out of the
way, and then, at his leisure, and in the privacy of his own
office, open the trunk and make the substitution.”

“But Ridgeway had the trunk with him!”

“Exactly. Ridgeway had the trunk. But where was the trunk before
it was taken to the station? In the Bank, of course. And who had
access to it? Why, the two managers. It was the simplest thing in
the world for Mr. Shaw to make the substitution then.”

“But the lock—why was it scratched and cut?”

“To make it look like an attempted robbery on board, of course!
The thief, having the key, would naturally use it, but he would
also want to make it look as if he hadn’t had the key. So he
scratched the lock.”

“But why did he wait until the _Olympia_ was almost at New York?”

“Because he wanted to be sure that the bonds would be sold before
the theft was discovered. If the theft had been discovered
earlier, the numbers of the bonds would have been broadcasted, and
it would have been impossible to sell them.”

“I see. And the invalid, Mr. Ventnor?”

“Was Mr. Shaw, of course! He was not ill at all. He was on board
the _Olympia_, in the cabin next to Ridgeway’s. He wanted to be on
the spot to make sure that everything went off as he had planned.
He could easily have slipped into Ridgeway’s cabin when the latter
was at dinner, and made the scratches on the lock. Then he could
have thrown the dummy package overboard, so that it should not be
found in his possession if he were searched.”

“But he was searched!”

“Of course he was. But he had nothing on him. The bonds were
already in New York, and the dummy package was at the bottom of
the Atlantic. He had only to walk off the boat and join his
accomplice.”

“It’s incredible!” I exclaimed. “And yet, it all fits in. But how
did you know about Mr. Ventnor?”

“I didn’t. I only knew that there must have been someone on board
who was interested in the trunk. And when I found that there was
an invalid in the next cabin who had hardly been seen during the
voyage, I knew I had found my man. A very simple case, Hastings,
as I told you.”

“And Miss Farquhar?”

“She will be very happy, I think. Her Philip’s character is
cleared, and she can now marry him with a clear conscience.”

“And Mr. Shaw?”

“He will, I hope, be enjoying the hospitality of one of His
Majesty’s prisons before very long. I have told Inspector McNeil
all about him, and I have no doubt he will be arrested this
evening.”

“Well, Poirot,” I said, “I must take off my hat to you. You’ve
certainly done it this time.”

“It is nothing, my friend, nothing. A simple application of the
little grey cells, that is all.”

“Think, Hastings! Who could have known the contents of the package,
and could have replaced them with a dummy? Who, but the person who
packed it? The two managers of the Bank, Mr. Vavasour and Mr.
Shaw! Now, why should they do such a thing? To save their own
pockets, _bien entendu_! The Bank is in difficulties—perhaps as
the result of their own speculations. They must have money. The
theft of the bonds would provide it. But it was essential that the
blame should fall on someone else. On Philip Ridgeway, the person
who had the care of the package.”

“But they both couldn’t have done it?”

“No. One of them, only one, was needed. And which one? Mr. Vavasour,
who was at the Bank all the time? Or Mr. Shaw, who was conveniently
absent with ‘bronchitis’?”

“Mr. Shaw!” I cried.

“Exactly. Mr. Shaw, who, as Mr. Ventnor, followed Philip Ridgeway
on the _Olympia_—taking care to be seen as little as possible. It
was he who, having a duplicate key to the trunk, could easily have
removed the dummy package and thrown it overboard—after making a
great show of trying to force the lock, to create the impression
of a common thief. That explains why he was the last to leave the
ship; he had to make sure the coast was clear.”

“Wait, wait! I proceed with my logical deduction. The package
could not have contained the bonds. Therefore, it contained—let us
say—a bundle of waste paper. But it had been sealed by the Bank
authorities. How was that managed? Not by a clerk—oh, no! For it
had been sealed in the presence of Mr. Ridgeway. That brings us to
the two joint general managers. If the package contained waste
paper, then it must have been prepared by one of these two
gentlemen, and handed to Ridgeway instead of the real package. Now,
is that possible? Could one of them have had access to the seals
and the wax—yes, but it would have been necessary to have the
other’s seal as well. And they are kept in a safe, of which each
man holds a key. Could one of them have obtained the other’s key?
Possibly, but it would have been difficult. Now, what happened?
One of the two managers was ill for a fortnight. That meant that
his colleague had both keys and could have prepared the package at
his leisure. Which of the two was ill? Mr. Shaw. Therefore, the
guilty person was Mr. Shaw.”

“But,” I cried, “the bonds were sold in New York before the boat
got in!”

“Wait. Consider the situation. A million dollars’ worth of bonds
to be sent to New York. If the package contained only dummy
papers, what had become of the real bonds? They were in the Bank,
in the care of the joint general managers. One of them, Mr. Shaw,
was conveniently ill at the time, and had been for a fortnight
previously. He had one of the three keys of the safe, and he alone
ordered the lock from Hubbs’s. What was to prevent him from
substituting a dummy package for the real one, and sending his
nephew off on a fool’s errand, while he himself disposed of the
bonds?”

“But he was ill in bed!”

“Was he? Or was he on board the _Olympia_ in the character of the
invalid Mr. Ventnor in cabin C 24, conveniently next to that of
his nephew? He had a duplicate key to the trunk, of course. He
takes out the dummy package, scratches the lock to make it look
like a clumsy attempt at a robbery, and then——”

“Yes?”

“Throws the package overboard!”

“And the bonds?”

“He had them with him, and his confederates in New York were
notified by cable to be ready to dispose of them the moment he
landed. As Mr. Ventnor, he was one of the last to leave the ship,
thus giving him plenty of time to avoid any possible recognition.”

“But how could he have got to Liverpool and on board the ship if
he was supposed to be ill in bed?”

“My dear Hastings, a man who is supposed to be in bed with
bronchitis does not usually have his doctor to see him every day.
A confederate, possibly a trusted servant, could easily have
managed the business for him.”

“Then it was Mr. Shaw after all!”

“Precisely. He was the only person who could have carried out the
whole scheme from start to finish. His illness was a very clever
stroke; it provided him with an alibi and at the same time gave
him the opportunity to be away from the Bank without exciting
suspicion.”

“And what about the duplicate key?”

“He ordered the lock himself, remember. It would have been easy
for him to have a duplicate key made at the same time. The whole
thing was beautifully planned, but he made one mistake.”

“What was that?”

“He forgot that Hercule Poirot has a memory for faces. I
recognised him the moment I saw him in the Bank, in spite of his
clean-shaven face and his grey hair. You see, Hastings, I had seen
his photograph in the paper some years ago in connection with a
charity committee, and I never forget a face.”

I looked at Poirot in admiration.

“You really are amazing, Poirot,” I said. “I should never have
thought of that.”

“It is my business to think of these things, Hastings,” he
replied, with a modest shrug of his shoulders. “And now, let us go
and meet Miss Farquhar. I think she will be very pleased to hear
the news.”

“Listen to my theory of the case. It is that the bonds never left
London at all. One of the joint general managers of the London and
Scottish Bank is the thief. He has access to the bonds, and it is
perfectly easy for him to substitute a package containing dummy
papers. The package is duly sealed in the presence of the other
manager and the unsuspecting Ridgeway. This manager has also
provided himself with a Hubbs’s key, and when he thinks his victim
sufficiently off his guard, he unlocks the trunk and takes the
package. He then proceeds to throw it overboard through the
porthole of his cabin.”

“But how could he be on board, if he stayed in London?” I cried.

“He did not stay in London. He followed Ridgeway, on the 23rd, by
the very same boat. He was ‘Mr. Ventnor,’ the invalid gentleman
of cabin C 24!”

“But which of them? Mr. Vavasour or Mr. Shaw?”

“Neither, _mon ami_. The thief was the man who had the best
opportunity to dispose of the bonds in New York while the _Olympia_
was still at sea—or rather, just as she arrived. The bonds were
sold, you remember, _before_ the ship docked. That means the thief
was already in New York!”

“But how? You said he was on the boat!”

“He was. But he didn't stay on it. Remember the 'invalid' who was the last to leave? That was a blind. The real thief had already slipped away. And who had the motive? Who was 'taken ill' just as the bonds were sent? Mr. Shaw!”

"But Shaw was in London, ill with bronchitis!"

"Was he? Or was that the perfect alibi? While Vavasour thought his colleague was in bed, Shaw was on the _Olympia_ in a wig and glasses. He slipped off the boat early—perhaps with the pilot or a mail boat—and sold the bonds before Ridgeway even knew they were gone. The 'invalid' seen later was merely a hired double or a clever ruse to make it seem the passenger was still aboard. Shaw is our man!"

“Permit me to continue. The last moment that the bonds are seen as
bonds is in the office of the London and Scottish Bank on the
morning of the 23rd. They reappear in New York half an hour after
the _Olympia_ gets in, and according to one man, whom nobody
listens to, actually _before_ she gets in. Supposing then, that
they have never been on the _Olympia_ at all? Is there any other
way they could get to New York? Yes. The _Gigantic_ leaves
Southampton on the same day as the _Olympia_, and she holds the
record for the Atlantic. Mailed by the _Gigantic_, the bonds would
be in New York the day before the _Olympia_ arrived. All is clear,
the case begins to explain itself. The sealed packet is only a
dummy, and the moment of its substitution must be in the office in
the Bank. It would be an easy matter for any of the three men
present to have prepared a duplicate package which could be
substituted for the genuine one. _Très bien_, the bonds are mailed
to a confederate in New York, with instructions to sell as soon as
the _Olympia_ is in, but some one must travel on the _Olympia_ to
engineer the supposed moment of the robbery.”

“But why?”

“Because that is the whole point of the scheme. The robbery is
meant to appear to have been committed on board the _Olympia_.
The trunk was scratched and cut about—that was to draw attention
to it. The thief, whoever he was, _had_ the key of the trunk, but
he knew it would be a much more convincing affair if he tried to
break it open first. He was probably an official of the Bank. The
joint manager, for instance.”

“But they were both in London!”

“Were they? One of them was—Mr. Vavasour. But the other, Mr. Shaw,
had been away from the Bank for a fortnight. He had bronchitis.
He had it so badly that he could see no one. But he was well
enough to take a voyage to New York, and to hide his identity under
the name of Mr. Ventnor in the cabin next to that of Philip
Ridgeway. It was he who took the dummy packet from Ridgeway’s trunk
and threw it overboard. He had the key—he had had it since the
23rd, when he had it made. His confederate in New York had already
received the bonds by the _Gigantic_ and was only waiting for a
cable from Shaw to say that the dummy packet had been disposed of
to begin his sales.”

“Then it was Shaw?” I cried.

“It was Shaw. He is now, I trust, in the hands of the police. It
was a clever, well-thought-out piece of work, but he made one
mistake. He should not have been so long in getting off the boat.
A man who had been a great invalid all the way across would naturally
be one of the first to land. He would not wait until the very last.”

Poirot sighed.

“I find it very sad, Hastings, that a man of his age should take
to crime. But as I said, the case was almost too easy. One had
only to use the little grey cells.”

“Because otherwise we should know that they had been stolen in the
office, and the three men present would come under suspicion. As
it is, it is the _unfortunate_ Ridgeway who is blamed. But how
could any of the three travel on the _Olympia_? Two of them were
needed for the business of the Bank, and the third was too ill to
leave his room. It is a _passe-partout_—a pass-key, what you call
it? Mr. Shaw’s illness. I ask myself, is he really ill? I see
a man, Mr. Ventnor, who is ill on the _Olympia_. Is he Mr. Shaw?
The description of him as an elderly gentleman with glasses who
hardly moved out of his cabin—is it not also a description of
Mr. Shaw? And then, the final and most significant clue: why should
the thief waste his time in trying to force a lock for which he
had the key? Obviously, because he wanted to make sure that the
theft should be discovered on the boat. He could have opened the
trunk, taken the packet, and relocked it—but then the loss might
not have been found out for days. No, the scratches and the forced
lock were necessary to fix the time and place of the crime. Mr.
Shaw, under the name of Ventnor, travels on the _Olympia_, and
at the right moment he removes the dummy packet from the trunk
and throws it overboard. His confederate in New York has already
received the real bonds by the faster _Gigantic_ and begins
selling them.”

“And it was Mr. Shaw?” I gasped. “But he was one of the managers!”

“To provide a motive—the theft of the bonds. Otherwise it would
be assumed that the bonds were missing from the Bank and the theft
would be traced to London. For this purpose, it was necessary to
have an accomplice on board—the mysterious Mr. Ventnor of the next
cabin, who, as we have seen, had every opportunity for making the
supposed attempt on the lock of the trunk, and who, when he had
obtained the dummy package, would simply throw it overboard. No
doubt he took with him a duplicate key of the trunk, and the
clumsy attempt to force the lock was only a ‘blind’ to satisfy the
eye. My friend, the culprit is—Mr. Shaw!”

I stared at him in amazement.

“Mr. Shaw? But he was ill with bronchitis!”

“Aha, _mon ami_, so we were told. But was he? The day he was taken
ill was the day the bonds were sent. What more easy than for him
to have caught the _Olympia_ at Liverpool, and to have appeared
on board as the invalid Mr. Ventnor? The grey hair, the glasses,
the secluded life in his cabin—all these were part of the
disguise. His colleague, Mr. Vavasour, was no doubt quite
unconscious of the deception. It was a clever plot, but it failed
to deceive Hercule Poirot!”

“To give the thief time to realize on the bonds. To put it
briefly, the theft must be a _fait accompli_ some time before the
_Olympia_ arrives. The thief must be someone who was present at
the sealing of the bonds, who had access to the keys and who could
reproduce the special lock of the trunk. It must be someone who
could conveniently disappear for a fortnight. The bronchitis of
Mr. Shaw, was it not convenient? He stays at home, while his
confederate, the mysterious Mr. Ventnor, a man with a grey beard
and spectacles, travels on the _Olympia_ in the cabin next to
Philip Ridgeway. He has provided himself with a duplicate key,
and at the first opportunity he enters Ridgeway’s cabin, and
begins to force the lock of the trunk. He knows he cannot do it,
but he wants to leave traces of an attempted robbery. Then,
_sapristi_, he finds he has the key after all! He opens the trunk,
takes out the package, and at the first opportunity he throws it
overboard. He stays in his cabin, a miserable invalid, until the
last moment, then he slips away in the crowd. He has nothing to
fear, he is not a thief, he has stolen nothing. The bonds are
already in New York. He has only to return to London and become
once more the respectable Mr. Shaw, who has been so ill with
bronchitis.”

“But the bonds?” I cried. “What about the bonds?”

“They were in the hands of the New York confederate, who was no
other than Mr. Shaw’s own son! A most talented family, the Shaws.
I have just had a wire from McNeil. They have arrested Mr. Shaw
at his house in Putney. He was just about to leave for a ‘convalescence’
in the South of France.”

“And the bonds?”

“I have no doubt they will be recovered in New York. A very neat
case, Hastings, but as I said, almost too simple for a mind like
mine!”

“The robbery must be discovered before the boat gets to New York,
so as to give the confederate time to dispose of the stolen
bonds—which he could not do if they were only missed when she got
in. So the thief has to have a cabin next to Ridgeway’s. He must
be a person who could have access to the Bank’s keys, and who could
get away from London for a time. Mr. Vavasour was at the Bank all
the time. Mr. Shaw was ‘ill’ with bronchitis for a fortnight. What
more simple? He buys a theatrical outfit, goes to Liverpool,
embarks on the _Olympia_ as Mr. Ventnor, and returns to London as
Mr. Shaw. But he made one mistake. He was too anxious to be
realistic. He was not content with opening the trunk with a
duplicate key—he must needs try to force the lock as well! It was
that that first gave me the clue. It was a most artistic touch,
but it was an artistic touch that failed.”

“And the bonds?” I asked.

“The bonds? Ah, I have no doubt that the good Inspector McNeil
will find them in Mr. Shaw’s possession—or what is left of them.
For the moment, however, we will keep his little secret to
ourselves and—_voilà_ Miss Farquhar! We will have a very pleasant
dinner.”

“Because if Ridgeway merely opens the packet and finds it a dummy,
suspicion flies at once to London. No, the man on board in the
cabin next door does his work, pretends to force the lock in an
obvious manner so as to draw immediate attention to the theft,
really unlocks the trunk with a duplicate key, throws the package
overboard and waits until the last to leave the boat. Naturally he
wears glasses to conceal his eyes, and is an invalid since he does
not want to run the risk of meeting Ridgeway. He steps ashore in
New York and returns by the first boat available.”

“But who—which was he?”

“I have not yet seen the gentleman, Hastings. But it is very
certain that he was not Mr. Vavasour, for he has been working at
the Bank ever since the 23rd, nor was it Philip Ridgeway, for he
was the victim, and besides, he was on board the _Olympia_ as
himself. There remains—one other. Mr. Shaw, who was ‘taken ill’
on the very day of the sailing, and who only recovered in time to
receive us. A very convenient illness, was it not? The description
of the elderly invalid tallies exactly with Mr. Shaw, even to the
fact that he is clean-shaven. He had only to provide himself with
a grey wig and spectacles, and the trick was done. He is the true
culprit who abused his position of trust to rob the Bank he
served. But here is the restaurant, and there is Miss Farquhar.
We must tell her the good news that her Philip is cleared of all
suspicion!”

“The man who ordered the lock and who, therefore, had the easiest
opportunity of getting a duplicate key made. The man who was
conveniently ‘ill’ for a fortnight, during which time he was
voyaging to New York and back. Our friend Mr. Shaw! And there, if
I am not mistaken, is Miss Farquhar, and I have the honour of
conveying to her the news that her fiancé is cleared and that the
actual thief is—even now—at the Yard.”

“That is the question, Hastings. The two joint managers, Mr.
Vavasour and Mr. Shaw. Only one of them was seen to be ill on the
day of the sailing, a most convenient bronchitis that kept him
from the office for a fortnight. It was Mr. Shaw who ordered the
lock from Hubbs's, and he who had the duplicate key. The invalid,
Mr. Ventnor, was Mr. Shaw himself, who had safely mailed the bonds
to New York by the *Gigantic* before ever the *Olympia* left
Liverpool. A simple case, as I said, but one that required the
ordered mind of Hercule Poirot to perceive the significance of a
man who is too ill to work, yet well enough to travel!”

“Why, Mr. Shaw, of course! Did he not tell us that he had been
suffering from severe bronchitis, and that it was no joke for a
man of his age? He was absent from the Bank for a fortnight. He
himself ordered the lock from Hubbs’s, and so would find it quite
easy to have a duplicate key made. He is now, I trust, safely in
the hands of Inspector McNeil, who will have some few questions
to put to him regarding his health and his whereabouts on the 23rd.”

I saw then that it was as Poirot said. Shaw, the joint general
manager of the Bank, was the thief. And the clue of the forced
lock had after all been the means of his undoing. For, as Poirot
had said, why should any one who had a key waste time in trying
to force an unforceable lock? Only to make certain that the theft
was discovered before the end of the voyage.

“The joint general manager who was fortunately taken ill—Mr. Shaw!
He is the only one who could have ordered the lock and thus
obtained a duplicate key. His ‘illness’ was a convenient blind for
his absence from London. The bonds were in his pocket all the
time, and he himself mailed them by the _Gigantic_. I have just
handed over to the Inspector the address of the New York broker
through whom they were sold, and which I was fortunate enough to
obtain by a little—how shall I say it?—_espionage_ at the Bank
to-day. As to Miss Farquhar, she will be waiting for us, and I
think we shall have a very pleasant dinner!”

“The man who had a duplicate key, the man who ordered the lock,
the man who has _not_ been severely ill with bronchitis at his home
in the country—_enfin_, that ‘stodgy’ old man, Mr. Shaw! There are
criminals in high places sometimes, my friend. Ah, here we are.
Mademoiselle, I have succeeded! You permit?”

And, beaming, Poirot kissed the astonished girl lightly on either
cheek!
